keywords: Toolbox for the Modeling and Analysis of Thermodynamic Systems
results.title: Incorporating Thermal Effects Into the Toolbox for the Modeling and Analysis of Thermodynamic Systems (T-MATS)
results.abstract: The Toolbox for the Modeling and Analysis of Thermodynamic Systems (T-MATS) has been a useful tool to facilitate system modeling and research for aero-propulsion systems. The toolbox was developed at the NASA Glenn Research Center and released publicly in 2016. Much of the publicized work utilizing T-MATS has involved the development of transient system-level models of turbomachinery-based propulsion systems for dynamics and controls research. T-MATS is well equipped to model engine shaft speed dynamics but is not readily able to incorporate thermal effects, which can account for a significant portion of the operability and performance variation of turbomachinery in aircraft engines. Recently, the capability of capturing nonadiabatic performance and operability impacts in compressors and turbines was added to T-MATS. This paper details the modeling methods used and demonstrates the new modeling tools through an application to a publicly available engine system model. The aim is to facilitate future research at NASA and throughout the greater aerospace community.

results.title: Single-Event Effects Test Report Crane Aerospace & Electronics cMOR2812D/ES and rMOR2812D/ES Dual DC/DC Converters
results.abstract: This study was undertaken to determine the single event effect susceptibility of the rMOR and cMOR dual DC-DC converters (cMOR2812D/ES and rMOR2812D/ES) manufactured by Crane Aerospace and Electronics, with emphasis on obtaining higher linear energy transfer (LET) data on both parts. The device was monitored for destructive events and significant voltage transients during exposure to a heavy ion beam at Lawrence Berkeley National Labs’ 88” Cyclotron.

results.title: Rain-to-Snow Transition: Evaluation of Precipitation Phase Algorithms in Southern New England
results.abstract: As part of the NASA’s Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) ground validation program, a multi-year winter field study in Storrs, Connecticut brought a unique opportunity to study the long-lasting problem of determination of precipitation phase of precipitation in precipitation products. This study evaluates the phase algorithms of NASA’s Integrated Multi-satellite Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) dataset, the flagship GPM global precipitation product, and NOAA’s Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) dataset, which is frequently used to validate IMERG precipitation rates over the continental United States. The study selected ten long-lasting phase transition events where rain and snow were recorded for more than one 30 hour with the presence of mixed precipitation and focused on two diverse events. The critical range of rain-to-snow transition has been identified a Twet value between -1˚C and 2˚C for both observed phase transitions and the performance of MRMS and IMERG phase algorithms. Using the PARSIVEL disdrometer phase as a ground truth, phase transition occurs at a mean Twet of 0.5˚C, which is in agreement with prior studies. IMERG and MRMS phase algorithms performed better when using HRRR, ERA5 temperatures than MERRA2 temperatures. Overall, IMERG version 07 performed better than its predecessor version 06. This study suggests that the IMERG snapshots show more snowy areas than it occurs. This study also evaluated HRRR deterministic and probabilistic phase algorithms, which performed better than HRRR temperature-based MRMS and IMERG algorithms, respectively.

results.title: Optical Transmitter FPGA Manual
results.abstract: The NASA Glenn Research Center developed a field programmable gate array (FPGA) implementation of a transmitter compatible with the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) Optical Communications High Photon Efficiency (HPE) standard. This manual describes the implementation. The HPE waveform was implemented on and ported to several platforms - the AMD Virtex-7 VC707 and Kintex Ultrascale+ KCU116 evaluation boards.

results.title: Barium Fluoride as a Standard Reference Material for Infrared Refractometry
results.abstract: This work proposes a standard reference material (SRM) for measurements of refractive index in the infrared spectral region (1–12 μm). The purpose of this material is to enable cross-method comparison of refractive index data obtained through minimum deviation, ellipsometry, interferometry, and prism coupling techniques. This will allow vendors and metrology laboratories, regardless of which technique they employ, to certify that their measurements meet required levels of accuracy, precision, and repeatability. Drawing on foundational work by Tilton at the National Bureau of Standards, a figure of merit for candidate SRM materials is outlined, and three materials are selected for further evaluation. Ultimately, barium fluoride is proposed as the most suitable SRM for the infrared spectral region, based on its broad transmission range, chemical and mechanical stability, low temperature dependence of refractive index, and well-characterized dispersion behavior.

results.title: CFD-Assisted Nodal Modeling of Sloshing in a Cryogenic Propellant Tank
results.abstract: During autogenous pressurization, tank sloshing causes a significant increase in pressurant consumption to maintain constant ullage pressure during draining of the tank. This increase in pressurant consumption is caused by a significant increase in condensation at the liquid-vapor interface. Sloshing strongly affects the liquid side heat transfer coefficient and thereby the condensation rate. Traditionally, sloshing is modeled by CFD code using the VOF (Volume of Fluid) method to track the liquid vapor interface during sloshing. CFD calculations require a very fine grid to accurately compute the heat and mass transfer at the interface. Therefore, computations are time consuming and prohibit performing many parametric studies often needed during the design of a new system. This paper describes an alternative approach by developing a CFD-assisted nodal model to predict system parameters more economically with reasonable accuracy. In this approach, a multi-node model of tank pressurization was developed using GFSSP. A multi-node model was needed to account for stratification. The model computes heat and mass transfer at the interface to calculate the condensation rate. The liquid side heat transfer is computed using the parameters of sloshing dynamics such as frequency, wave amplitude, and interface area. The parameters of sloshing dynamics are computed by the CFD code LOCI-Stream. The model predictions were compared with test data for several cases.

results.title: Petermann Glacier on the Brink: Progress, Challenges and Insights

organization.name: Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland
Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland
Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland

results.abstract: Petermann Glacier, the largest marine-terminating glacier in northern Greenland based on catchment area and ice discharge, plays a key role in regulating ice discharge from the Greenland Ice Sheet into the Arctic Ocean. With an upstream catchment connected to the ice sheet interior via a deep subglacial canyon, its future stability has major implications for sea level rise. In this review, we synthesize recent advances in understanding Petermann’s dynamics across three critical interfaces: the ice–ocean, ice–atmosphere, and ice–bed boundaries. At the surface, observations show that reanalysis products underestimate air temperatures and melt, while regional climate models diverge significantly in their estimates of surface mass balance, underscoring the need for improved in situ data and models. At the ocean boundary, enhanced basal melting driven by both subglacial runoff and Atlantic water intrusions is identified as the dominant driver of recent mass loss of Petermann Glacier, with continued warming posing a serious threat to the stability of the floating tongue. At the bed, new geophysical synthesis reveals complex geology, likely spatial variability in geothermal heat flux, and the influence of the megacanyon on seasonal hydrology and velocity fluctuations. Petermann’s mass balance has been negative in recent decades without corresponding flow acceleration. However, the glacier has undergone significant calving events, and the current rifting that began in September 2025 highlights its vulnerability. This upcoming calving event underscores the timeliness of this review, as it will put Petermann Glacier’s terminus at its most retreated position since records began in 1923. The anticipated retreat of the ice tongue also reduces buttressing and brings the terminus closer to the grounding zone, and modeling studies suggest that calving within 12 km of the grounding zone could potentially trigger dynamic retreat, accelerating ice discharge, and a doubling of flow speeds. We conclude that improved observations, sustained monitoring of oceanographic and atmospheric properties, and high-resolution modeling are critical to constraining projections of Petermann Glacier’s future and its role in the stability of the Greenland Ice Sheet.

results.title: A Multi-Tier Autonomous Aerial Architecture for Wildfire Detection, Characterization, and Communication in Infrastructure-Denied Environments
results.abstract: Wildfire response depends on how fast an ignition can be confirmed and located, especially in remote regions where ground-based communication and monitoring may be limited. Geostationary sensors provide frequent observations but at kilometer-scale resolution, which is too coarse to resolve small fires in remote terrain. Ground camera networks require sightlines and infrastructure that back-country areas lack. To address these limitations, this work proposes a Multi-Tier Autonomous Wildfire Intelligence System that combines wide-area monitoring with targeted, high-resolution sensing. A solar-powered high-altitude long endurance (HALE) platform operating at approximately 60,000 ft provides persistent wide-area thermal and optical surveillance, running onboard edge inference to screen candidate ignitions and reduce false positives and downlink bandwidth. When a candidate ignition is detected, low-altitude uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS) can be deployed to conduct localized observations, including high-resolution imaging and atmospheric measurements such as wind and plume observation. By combining persistent detection with local sensing, the proposed architecture is designed to provide first responders with timely, high-resolution information about fire location and behavior to aid in emergency decision making.

results.title: Suborbital Lidar to Profile Temperature and Salinity in the Ocean Across Synoptic Scales: Advancing Ocean Observations in the 2028–2037 Decade
results.abstract:
High-resolution, rapidly acquired subsurface temperature and salinity measurements are critical for improving ocean models, yet remain difficult to obtain with current in-situ sensor networks. Dynamically complex regions like the Mid-Atlantic Bight particularly suffer from insufficient sampling density, limiting forecast skill for phenomena such as hurricane intensification. Brillouin lidar represents a promising technological solution to this observational gap. An aircraft-mounted Brillouin lidar system can survey the Mid-Atlantic Bight, or similar sensitive water bodies in ~8 hours, delivering measurements with both the spatial coverage and measurement precision needed to significantly advance regional ocean models.

Beyond hurricane forecasting, this capability enables multiple high-impact applications: monitoring flooding and pollution, resolving ocean fronts and eddies, fishery management, forecasting harmful algal blooms, enhancing model forecasting skill, and monitoring key climate variables. The system's ability to provide rapid, synoptic snapshots complements existing glider networks and in-situ platforms, filling a critical scale gap in coastal ocean observing. Advancing this technology through the Decadal Survey would establish airborne Brillouin lidar as a cornerstone ancillary observational tool for U.S. coastal science and marine forecasting.

results.title: Elevation-Dependent Hydrological Vulnerability of Lakes and Reservoirs to Evaporation Loss in the Yarlung Zangbo River Basin, Tibetan Plateau
results.abstract:
The Tibetan Plateau’s Yarlung Zangbo River Basin is undergoing rapid hydroclimatic transitions compounded by extensive reservoir development. Accurately quantifying evaporative water losses and water balance and interpreting their associated isotopic signatures is critical for improving hydrological models and regional water security assessment. In this study, we tested the application of an isotope-based Bayesian framework for quantifying evaporation and water balance dynamics. Utilizing steady-state models for the long-term water balance of natural lakes and transient models for the short-term water balance of artificial reservoirs, this framework calculated a unified mass-balance metric, the evaporative loss index (E/(E+Q)), where E represents evaporative water loss and Q denotes water outflow.
Results reveal that despite operating on different temporal scales, the inflow-dependent evaporative loss indices exhibit diametrically opposed altitudinal dependencies between lakes and reservoirs, which can substantially mask the natural riverine δ18O altitude effect. Natural lakes, for which evaporative loss index is functionally equivalent to the evaporation-to-inflow ratio under steady-state conditions, are found to have average values of 0.27 ± 0.19 and show a strong positive correlation with elevation. In high-altitude basins (> 4500 m a.s.l.), limited natural inflows cause substantial proportional evaporative losses relative to the water balance (mean E/(E+Q) = 0.51), highlighting severe hydrological vulnerability to evaporative loss despite low absolute evaporation rates. This intense fractionation can substantially modify the pristine cryospheric baseflow, acting as a contributing mechanism to the reversal of the steep negative gradient in localized surface waters.. Conversely, artifically-constructed reservoirs exhibit a negative altitudinal evaporative gradient, with evaporation accounting for 0.47 ± 0.16 of total water losses in low-elevation shallow basins during the dry season. Rapid downstream transport of water from high-altitude reservoirs disrupts and homogenizes natural isotopic gradients in rivers. This systematic disruption of natural isotopic baselines by both climate-driven evaporation and human water retention explicitly warns against utilizing uncorrected surface water isotopes for hydrological tracing or paleoaltimetry reconstructions. These findings highlight extreme vulnerabilities in regional water security, demanding altitude-specific management adaptations.

results.title: Entropy-Regularized Drift-Diffusion Solutions to the Compressible Navier-Stokes Equations: Exact Shock Structures in Gas and Liquid Media
results.abstract: The author presents a novel transformation of the compressible Navier-Stokes equations into an entropy-regularized drift-diffusion form, analytically solvable in flattened coordinates and directly validated against experimental data from classical and high-Mach shock phenomena in both gases and liquids. The resulting parabolic Fokker-Planck structure yields closed-form density and pressure solutions that reproduce sigmoid shock profiles and avoid singular behavior. The method is validated against Sod shock tubes, Mach 9 Argon data from Alsmeyer, and bubble collapse pressures from Liang et al., achieving strong physical and numerical agreement. The implications for the Clay Millennium problem on Navier-Stokes completeness are also discussed.

results.title: B&P Project 25-3: Regolith Gas Permeability Tester Project (REGAPT2)
results.abstract:
Regolith particles accelerated by gases from plume-surface interactions (PSI) during the
descent and landing of a lander vehicle on the Moon represent a potential risk to the sustainable human
exploration of the lunar surface. However, the nature of gas flow through granular materials also has broad implications across many fields. For example, gases escaping from the interior of comets permeate through regolith to create a coma around the nucleus and a tail of primordial dust; gas volatiles liberated from planetary surfaces for in situ resource utilization must diffuse through regolith; and gas has been used in touch-and-go sample acquisition maneuvers to excite asteroid regolith into collection pads. The permeability of regolith is additionally important when considering the construction of subterranean habitats. This FY25 Research and Technology (R&T) project at NASA KSC focused on measuring the gas permeability of granular lunar regolith simulant material in support of the Human Landing System (HLS) PSI project (see https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20230018215). For each HLS PSI ground test case (or computational modeling of PSI effects), the gas permeability of lunar regolith is a fundamentally important parameter needed to understand the efficiency of gas flow in producing plume-surface interaction effects during a lunar landing.

results.title: Novel Calibration Method for Seven-Hole Probes
results.abstract: This work describes a novel method to calibrate seven-hole probes using open-source software packages. The new software is written in Python so it can easily be run and maintained at facilities including those at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Seven-hole probes are used to measure flow parameters such as Mach number, pitch or yaw angles and are not as straightforward as one might think in their practical utilization. When seven-hole data quality is in question, it is sometimes difficult to identify the underlying cause. In fact, existing Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) solutions used currently at NASA are increasingly using encryption to prevent end-users from accessing calibration data or algorithms employed to reduce the pressure data into flow parameters. The novel method devised in this work is used to validate results obtained from the available COTS solution. While it should apply to compressible subsonic flows, it is currently only demonstrated for flows where the Mach number (M) is less than 0.3. The method is limited to cone angles less than 60°. It is intended to be tested and validated over a larger range of Mach numbers in the near future with in-house calibration data collected in partnership with the Advanced Measurements and Flow Physics branch at the NASA Langley Research Center.

results.title: 2025 Long-Term Monitoring Report for the Fluid Servicing Road Area
results.abstract:
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), through its Environmental Assurance Branch, is managing cleanup of two sites through the Fluid Servicing Road Area
(FSRA) Long-Term Monitoring (LTM) program at the John F. Kennedy Space Center (KSC), Florida. The FSRA LTM program includes two sites, the Former Drum Storage Area (FDSA),
Solid Waste Management Unit (SWMU) 037 and the Propellants Support Building Area (PSBA), SWMU 102. The sites are monitored under KSC’s Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) Corrective Action Program.The activities presented in this report include the May 2025 biennial groundwater monitoring well sampling conducted at FDSA and PSBA and the November 2025 semi-annual groundwater monitoring well sampling conducted at FDSA. AECOM Technical Services, Inc. (AECOM) prepared this report and completed LTM activities for the FSRA LTM program sites for NASA under Contract 80KSC024DA001, Task Order 80KSC024FA117.

The FDSA site is currently sampled on a semi-annual, annual, and biennial frequency. The site contaminants of concern (COCs) are tetrachloroethene (PCE); trichloroethene (TCE); cis-1,2-dichloroethene (cDCE); trans-1,2-dichloroethene (tDCE); 1,1-dichloroethene (1,1-DCE); and vinyl chloride (VC). Water levels confirm groundwater flow directions for each depth interval remain consistent with historical observations. LTM data demonstrate that TCE and VC concentrations at FDSA remain stable or decreasing when compared with historical results; however, there were several increases in TCE concentrations during the 2025 sampling event at several monitoring wells when compared to recent sampling events in which trends should be thoroughly monitored during future evaluations. LTM data indicates that cDCE concentrations at FDSA are increasing in several monitoring wells when compared to recent historical results; suggesting that attenuation processes are occurring and that site conditions are suitable for continued LTM. The next annual sampling event is scheduled for November 2026, and the next biennial sampling event is scheduled for May 2027.

The PSBA is currently sampled on an annual and biennial frequency. The site COCs are TCE, cDCE, tDCE, and VC. Water levels confirm groundwater flow directions for each depth interval remain consistent with historical observations. LTM data demonstrate that VC concentrations at PSBA continue to remain stable or decrease, suggesting that attenuation processes are occurring and that site conditions are suitable for continued LTM. The next annual sampling event is scheduled for November 2026, and the next biennial sampling event is scheduled for May 2027.

results.title: SomBench: Benchmark Dataset for Advancing Machine Learning in Lunar Science

organization.name: The University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH)
IBM Research - Thomas J. Watson Research Center
IBM Research - Thomas J. Watson Research Center
IBM Research - Thomas J. Watson Research Center
IBM Research - Thomas J. Watson Research Center

results.abstract: Lunar orbital missions, such as Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, Kaguya/SELENE, Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory, and Lunar Prospector, among others, provide rich multi-instrument observations, but their heterogeneity in sampling, projection, and conventions limits reproducible machine learning (ML). We introduce SomBench, a unified, spatially-aligned, ML-ready lunar dataset aggregating 30+ co-registered layers from ten instruments across four missions, spanning 1m to 20km/pixel and covering ±82° latitude in 90 Lunar Transverse Mercator zones with two polar stereographic caps. An image-anchored tiling pipeline yields pretraining-ready multimodal tile views with leakage-safe splits, distributed as netCDF with Parquet catalogs. An application benchmark suite spans impact processes, volcanic history, and polar volatiles. Baseline experiments with ResNet-50 and SwinV2-B models confirm that each benchmark task is learnable from the released inputs, establishing reference points for future model development.

results.title: Empowering K–12 Learners as Creators: Designing an Educator-Ready Sequence for Virtual, Place-Based Learning
results.abstract: Immersive interactive experiences like virtual field trips are increasingly popular in K-12 education, yet they often position youth as consumers. This paper details a design-based-research approach to developing a learning sequence that empowers students as creators of their own immersive learning experiences, grounded in principles of project- and place-based learning. An initial series of four case studies, involving six educators and 100+ youth, illustrates design milestones; highlighting that while students enjoy creating these experiences and educators recognize the pedagogical value, challenges such as time constraints and project scaffolding can impede implementation. Although these case studies represent small, non-controlled samples, findings were consistent across iterations. In response to these findings we present the VFT Creation Sequence, a suite of learning resources that uplifts the student experience and provides practical support for authentic implementation. A final case study showcases the sequence in practice in an elementary science classroom and examines domain-specific features of the student work, yielding promising results in using student products as evidence of sense-making. VFT creation can complement instruction across domains and learning contexts; the VFT Creation Sequence was designed to be easily distributed to and adapted by educators interested in integrating learner-driven digital activities into their curriculum.

results.title: Structured Quantum Kernels for Chaotic Forecasting

organization.name: Research Institute for Advanced Computer Science

results.abstract:
Quantum kernels promise exponentially large feature spaces, but expressive circuits concentrate their Gram matrices, bandwidth tuning collapses them toward classical RBF, and the practical consensus is that quantum kernels add nothing on classical data. We provide an answer to another productive question, an architectural one: whether the structure of an encoding circuit can carry an inductive
bias that tuned classical kernels lack. We introduce AeRot, a quantum kernel that fuses amplitude encoding of ℓ2-normalized delay windows with a grouped single-qubit rotation layer assigning contiguous temporal blocks to each qubit, making the circuit delay-window-aware. On Lorenz-63 non-autoregressive kernel ridge regression (KRR) with cross-validated bandwidths for 100 seeds, AeRot
outperforms tuned RBF and Matérn-5/2, with the advantage emerging at physical horizons ≥ 0.15 tu and reaching +0.137 mean R2 at 0.25 tu (5 qubits, N =32). Linear-stability analysis of the window tail shows the advantage concentrates in the locally unstable saddle-approach regime: AeRot wins 83% of windows in the most unstable decile, with the quantum-win rate scaling monotonically with tail instability and a sign flip at the local stability boundary ( ̄λtail ≈ 0). The difficulty is fold-branch ambiguity: trajectories approaching the saddle are locally diverging, and Euclidean kernels struggle to resolve which lobe the trajectory will commit to. Structural diagnostics confirm non-concentrated Gram matrices distinct from
tuned RBF (normalized Frobenius distance ≈ 0.44) and strictly higher target-kernel alignment at every horizon (95–100% of seeds). The gain is architectural: a finite sample inductive-bias effect of temporally structured encoding on a folded attractor, with no computational-separation claim attached. To our knowledge, this is the first mechanistic localisation of quantum-kernel advantage to a specific dynamical
regime of a classical system.

results.title: Beyond SMAP: Can GNSS-R Platforms Ensure Continuity of Global Soil Moisture Observations?

organization.name: Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology

results.abstract: The absence of a definitive follow-on strategy for the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) mission, which has already surpassed its planned mission lifetime, presents a significant challenge for the hydrological science community. GNSS-Reflectometry (GNSS-R), which exploits reflected satellite navigation signals, has emerged as a rapidly growing alternative for soil moisture retrieval, increasingly positioned as a low-cost path to global observation. The two approaches, however, differ fundamentally in how they sense the surface, and the hydrological science community should weigh these differences carefully before decisions are made that could compromise the continuity of this essential climate variable's data record. In this study, we compared soil moisture products from these two systems across seven perspectives: (a) observation characteristics, (b) spatial resolution, (c) coverage and frequency of observations, (d) vulnerability to radio frequency interference, (e) complementarity potential, (f) performance, and (g) cost considerations. Our assessment suggests that GNSS-R is better understood as a complement to SMAP than as a replacement. A GNSS-R constellation can deliver sub-daily observations, and lower upfront costs, capabilities that genuinely extend what single-platform missions can offer. At the same time, GNSS-R retrievals exhibit variable spatial sampling and canopy attenuation, and the highest-performing products are typically trained, calibrated, or benchmarked against SMAP (an implicit cost that the low-cost framing of GNSS-R does not fully capture). Taken together, these findings underscore the need for sustained investment in both SMAP-class L-band missions and the expanding GNSS-R constellation, each contributing complementarity strengths to a resilient global soil moisture observing system.

results.title: Spatially Refined Satellite Gravimetry Captures Human Signatures in Global Terrestrial Water Storage Trends
results.abstract: Human activities have directly altered the water cycle through water management, aquifer pumping, agricultural irrigation, and land use change. Although satellite gravimetry has transformed global hydrological research, its coarse resolution limits attribution of freshwater change to human activities at many management-relevant scales. Here we assessed global terrestrial water storage (TWS) trends from April 2002 to November 2025 using “stacked” regression of Level-1B intersatellite ranging data, which leverages temporal information and variability to dramatically improve effective spatial resolution relative to standard approaches. We combined this refined product with rigorous uncertainty analysis, autocorrelation-robust geostatistical methods, and literature assessment to evaluate TWS trend associations with land and water use, climate variability, and glacial mass loss. We identified TWS trend hotspots exhibiting significant spatial associations with anthropogenic 40 drivers, including groundwater and surface-water irrigation, rainfed agriculture, deforestation, and reservoir impoundment. Across these regions, cumulative TWS losses (3,122 Gt) substantially exceeded gains (2,432 Gt). Compared with traditional regression of monthly mascons, our approach yielded regional trend magnitudes that are on average 33% larger, revealing that global freshwater depletion, particularly from groundwater pumping, is considerably more acute than previously estimated. Multivariate regression models show that humans account for a significant share of the spatial variability in TWS trends on every non-polar continent except Australia. We detected localized TWS gains linked to rainfed agriculture, surface water irrigation, and reservoir filling that were unresolved in earlier gravimetric studies. The methodology provides a foundation for future gravity missions to independently track decadal freshwater change with unprecedented spatial fidelity.

results.title: The Application of A HACCP Informed Risk Assessment to Mizuna and Tomato Crops Grown on ISS in Veggie to Develop A Baseline Food Safety Plan Within the Constraints of Space Mission Food Production
results.abstract: The prevention of human and plant diseases is critical for a robust space crop production system.  We have applied a Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point HACCP framework to the cultivation of crops on the International Space Station (ISS) in the Veggie hardware to develop a baseline food safety plan that can help inform standards for crops grown within the limitations of spaceflight.  This plan was applied to the VEG-04 and VEG-05 experiments in which mizuna, and tomato were grown under different lighting and harvest regimes. Experiments were carried out in two Veggie facilities, one with a red-rich light recipe and one with blue-rich lighting, with corresponding ground control experiments conducted at Kennedy Space Center in ISS environmental simulators.  Potential human pathogens were not detected on plants grown in the VEG-04 and 05 experiments with the exception of S. aureus on one mizuna plant in VEG-04B. Pre-flight procedures for hardware and seed sanitization were identified as control points.  While the HACCP approach is applied here to VEG-04 and 05 crops, space crop production presents unique challenges in the monitoring and control that will require development of new technologies or methods to validate safety of foods grown in spaceflight.

results.title:
Computational and Experimental Comparison of CLF5605 and
Roamx-0201 Martian Helicopter Rotor Airfoils
results.abstract: This study compares performance of the CLF5605 rotor airfoil — which flew on Ingenuity— with that of a new optimized roamx-0201 airfoil designed for Martian conditions at NASA Ames Research Center. Specifically, performance is studied at a Reynolds number of 20,000 and a Mach number of 0.60, across a range of angles of attack. In this regime, flow can be highly sensitive to geometry and operating conditions, and results from computational analysis and physical testing can be strongly affected by small differences in setup. Accordingly, in order to achieve confidence in observed trends, the airfoils are studied using three independent state-of-the-art methodologies: implicit large eddy simulations using NASA’s OVERFLOW solver, direct numerical simulations using the high-order PyFR solver, and experimental testing in the Mars Wind Tunnel at Tohoku University. Across methodologies the roamx-0201 airfoil achieves a ∼ 19 − 43% improvement in lift-to-drag ratio relative to the CLF5605 airfoil. Moreover, OVERFLOW and PyFR results show that the roamx-0201 airfoil has superior stall characteristics, and can achieve a maximum lift ∼ 20% higher than the CLF5605 airfoil. The work provides a strong body of evidence to support further studies into use of rotors based on the optimized roamx-0201 airfoil for future Mars helicopter missions.

results.title: Regional Aerosol Emission Reductions Alter Tropical Circulation

organization.name: Korea Institute of Science & Technology Evaluation and Planning
Korea Institute of Science and Technology
CICERO Center for International Climate Research
The University of Texas at Austin

results.abstract: Anthropogenic aerosol emissions are projected to decline rapidly in the near future as air quality regulations strengthen. Crucially, however, the response of large-scale atmospheric circulation to these reductions remains a major source of uncertainty. Here, we use multi-model ensembles from Regional Aerosol Model Intercomparison Project to provide a diagnostic assessment of tropical circulation changes in response to global and regional aerosol reductions during 2015–2050. We find that global aerosol reductions lead to a poleward expansion of the Northern Hemisphere (NH) tropical width by 0.10° ± 0.08°, a weakening of the NH Hadley Circulation (HC) by 1.77 ± 1.09 109 kg s<sup>−1</sup> and a strengthening of the Southern Hemisphere HC by 2.53 ± 1.30 109 kg s<sup>−1</sup>. The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) also shows a northward shift by 0.19° ± 0.10°. These meridional circulation changes consistently emerge across the regional experiments, with aerosol reductions over East Asia and North America + Europe contributing the most. Although the response of the zonal Pacific Walker circulation to global aerosol reductions is not statistically significant, models show a strengthening tendency that is significant under Africa + Middle East aerosol reductions. Notably, the ITCZ response to greenhouse gas forcing is weak and uncertain, whereas aerosol reductions produce a stronger and more robust response, even in the regional experiments. Our results suggest that both global and regional aerosol reduction significantly contribute to large-scale tropical circulation changes.

results.title: Ion Thruster Plume Far-Field Wave-Particle Interactions with Solar Energetic Particles
results.abstract: While Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR) represent a long-term cancer risk to deep space human missions, Solar Energetic Particles (SEP) represent a significant acute radiation hazard. We investigate wave-particle interactions caused by the incidence of an energetic proton flux, representing a notional SEP event, onto a cloud of ions representing the far-field region of a notional ion thruster plume. The resulting instability is developed to investigate the potential wave growth rate and deflection of energetic protons out of the initial proton flux via pitch angle deflection, including dependence on incident SEP energy and flux, thruster ion energy, and orientation relative to SEP incidence. We investigate a potential technique to mitigate radiation hazards to interplanetary human spaceflight, and the overarching intent is to develop a concept that can merit subsequent investigation and future testing in the laboratory or in space. Since the cost in expended fuel restricts such a technique to intermittent use during interplanetary flights, effective prediction of when a SEP event might impact the mission is still important, and the observation of conditions that might lead to SEP events, human-in-the-loop space weather analyses, and development of SEP prediction models remain essential to crew safety, spacecraft function, and mission success.

results.title: A Simplified Higher Order Closure + Mass Flux Boundary-layer Parameterization in the Goddard Earth Observing System
results.abstract: Boundary-layer turbulence and clouds play an essential role in regulating surface fluxes and the Earth's radiative balance, but their parameterization in global models remains a significant source of uncertainty. This paper describes a novel implementation of the Simplified Higher Order Closure (SHOC) coupled with a multi-plume eddy diffusivity mass flux scheme in the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) model. The SHOC scheme provides eddy diffusivities and uses a set of higher order moments (HOMs) to constrain an analytic double Gaussian probability distribution function (PDF), from which the subgrid buoyancy flux and cloud properties are diagnosed. This SHOC + MF implementation extends previous work by including mass flux contributions to all HOMs, which remedies a significant underestimation of subgrid scale variances, and allows the combined convective and stratiform cloud properties to be diagnosed from the assumed PDF in a unified way. Single column experiments show the SHOC + MF scheme compares favorably to large eddy simulations in trade cumulus, marine stratocumulus, and continental convective boundary-layer regimes, relative to the default GEOS boundary-layer parameterizations. Global experiments show improvements in simulated clouds and surface stress. This study demonstrates the feasibility of a closer coupling between higher order closure and MF, and a unified representation of shallow clouds

results.title: Representing An Extreme Smoke Transport Event in the Goddard Earth Observing System: A Case Study for June 2023
results.abstract:
Aerosols emitted from biomass burning can have profound societal impacts and are harmful for
human health. With projected increases in wildfires and the associated fine particulate matter
(PM2.5), it is important to understand how well smoke transport events are represented and
forecasted within weather and aerosol transport models. Using the extreme event from June 2023 when wildfires in Alberta, Canada and Quebec, Canada resulted in unhealthy air quality conditions across the northeastern United States as a case study, different configurations of the NASA GEOS model are used to put the event in a historical perspective and determine processes and settings within the model that could be modified to result in more accurate forecasts in the future. Despite the assimilation of aerosol optical depth in the GEOS near real time forecasting system, forecasts of PM2.5 during the 5-day smoke transport event in early June were vastly overestimated at the onset of the event, while the temporal maximum in PM2.5 was mis-timed. Experiments were conducted to determine the impact of persisting emissions throughout the forecast window, an the role of plume rise for stronger fires that have smoke penetrating the boundary layer. Ultimately the assimilation of aerosol optical depth proved to have adverse impacts on the vertical profile of smoke within GEOS. The assimilation accommodated for insufficient emissions of biomass burning aerosol and placed smoke near the surface rather than aloft.

results.title: Strategic Pathways for Advancing In-Space Manufacturing of Metal Parts
results.abstract: In-space manufacturing (ISM) of discrete metal components presents a critical opportunity to reduce reliance on Earth-based supply chains, mitigate the risks of unforeseen hardware failures, and drastically decrease the launch mass dedicated to spare components. This white paper serves as a guide for future ISM efforts by assessing a wide range of metallic manufacturing processes within the existing Artemis, Moon Base, and future Mars mission frameworks. Through internal evaluation and industry consensus, this study ultimately recommends exploring several technologies for further development on a use-case-based down-selection process. Laser wire directed energy deposition (LW-DED) currently scores the highest among these, driven by its reduced gravity compatibility, build rate, manageable power requirements, extensibility to in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) for feedstocks, and the avoidance of hazards due to loose powder. To address resolution limitations of this and other existing technologies, a series of resolution improvement trials using in-situ monitoring and machine learning-enabled control are recommended. Improvement of build volume and rate, as well as material compatibility improvement are also recommended as investigations with the highest return on investment for multiple technologies. This review also considers and discusses the impact of vital ancillary technologies such as cleaning, heat treatment, subtractive post-processing, and non-destructive evaluation (NDE). Ultimately, the resulting analysis establishes a rating framework for ISM technologies, provides industry insights, makes process recommendations, and gives guidance on technology maturation, emphasizing the necessary paradigm shift toward data-driven, in-mission qualification to inform NASA’s long-term strategy for sustainable and logistically independent metal ISM capabilities.

results.title: Single-Scattering Look-Up Table for Remote Sensing and in Situ Black Carbon Studies
results.abstract:
Coupled atmosphere and ocean remote sensing retrievals
of microphysical properties made by the NASA Plankton,
Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission require
time-consuming single-scattering computations for the con-
stituents. Our line of look-up tables allows us to speed up
these computations for aerosols and cloud droplets in the
atmosphere, and for coated spheres representing oceanic
phytoplankton. In this study, we tabulate the computations
of the single-scattering properties of fractal-like aggregates
with a complex refractive index of 1.95–i⋅ 0.96, characteris-
tic of bare carbonaceous soot for wavelengths from 0.35 to
2.3 μm. Our new look-up table covers aggregates with frac-
tal dimensions of 1.4–2.8 consisting of 1 to 4,096 touching
black carbon monomers with identical radii in the range
0.015 to 0.025 μm. We achieve an increase of at least 106
in computational speed compared to direct calculations. As
an application example, we use our look-up table to re-
produce the low single-scattering albedo of in situ aerosol
measurements acquired during the NASA ACTIVATE mis-
sion.

results.abstract: A growing number of applications requires reaching a very high level of accuracy for the global terrestrial coordinate frame,  1 mm and 0.1 mm/yr stability. To meet this stringent accuracy  requirement is a serious challenge. We identified three major problems: 1) ties between reference points of collocated  instruments of different techniques determined with conventional  surveys have with significant biases; 2) reported uncertainties  of geodetic results are in most cases unrealistic; and  3) atmospheric turbulence sets the barrier in accuracy of  microwave geodetic techniques. We argue that solution of the  first problem is on the way using the emerging micro-VLBI  technique. Solving two latter problems will require  focused, collaborative efforts between geodesists and  atmospheric scientists.

results.title: Impact of Two Radio Occultation Constellations on Numerical Weather Prediction: Polar-Orbits Only and Mixed Polar-Equatorial Orbits
results.abstract:
This study explores the relative impact of two orbital configurations for Global Navigation Satellite System radio occultation (RO) observations in numerical weather prediction (NWP) using observing system simulation experiments (OSSE). Three experiments are carried out: a Control experiment with no RO observations and two experiments with 14,000 RO profiles per day - one with only polar orbiting satellites which provides a high concentration of profiles in the extratropics but has gaps in spatial coverage every six hours, and a second with a mix of polar and equatorial orbits with RO profiles that are more concentrated in the tropics and has a more uniform local time coverage. Both experiments with RO included show a marked increase in forecast accuracy compared to the Control. The mixed orbit case shows a significant improvement in forecast accuracy compared to the polar-only orbit case in the tropics. 

The OSSE framework allows calculation of observation impacts on background and analysis errors, so that the contribution of information from retained RO information can be compared with the contribution of new information from observations ingested in the current cycle. Impacts of RO in the two sampling experiments are also explored using a forecast sensitivity observation impact (FSOI) tool for 24-hour forecasts, and by comparing the skill of medium-range forecasts. In stratospheric midlatitudes, the RO observational information is well retained, so that more frequent sampling is not required. However, the Tropics are found to be particularly sensitive to RO data in both the stratosphere and troposphere, and relatively uniform coverage is advantageous.

results.title: Harnessing Wheat Germplasm to Sustain Grain-Filling Under Climate Warming Using A Gene-Based Modelling Framework

organization.name: Centro Internacional de Mejoramiento de Maíz Y Trigo

results.abstract: Rising temperatures accelerate wheat development and shorten grain-filling duration (GFD), thereby constraining yield formation. We hypothesized that harnessing wheat germplasm could sustain GFD and/or increase grain-filling rate (GFR) and enhance resilience to warming through optimized source-sink dynamics. Here, we first conducted genome-wide association studies on 163 diverse cultivars to identify stable loci associated with GFD and GFR. We then developed a gene-based modelling framework by deriving cultivar-specific parameters of the CERES-Wheat model from the identified stable loci using Random Forest (RF). Finally, we applied the framework across 45 global sites under current and future climates. Pyramiding favorable alleles could extend GFD by 11.4% and increase GFR by 14.8%, resulting in yield gains of up to 9.5% under irrigated conditions and 2.3% under rainfed conditions in mid-century RCP8.5 scenarios. GFR enhancement was most effective in high-rainfall environments, whereas GFD extension was more beneficial at water-limited sites. This gene-based modelling framework reveals how genetic control of grain-filling traits mediates genotype × environment × management (G×E × M) responses under climate change, providing a tool to test marker-assisted strategies toward climate-resilient cultivars.

results.title: Impacts of climate driven yield changes on the affordability of healthy diets: a modelling study

results.abstract: Food security is central to global nutrition improvement and public health goals, and healthy diets represent a higher-level aspiration beyond merely avoiding hunger. Climate change poses an increasing threat to food systems by affecting crop yields and food prices. Although climate change-driven risks to hunger have been widely studied, the extent to which climate change undermines the affordability of healthy diets while accounting for socioeconomic responses and regional inequalities remains insufficiently understood. This study aimed to quantify the effects of climate change on the future affordability of healthy diets under alternative socioeconomic and climate scenarios.

results.abstract: Rice sustains more than half of the world’s population and is produced across diverse ecosystems, including irrigated and rainfed lowlands, uplands, and deep-water systems. This diversity creates large differences in water management regimes, climate risks, feasible management responses, and environmental outcomes. As climate change intensifies heat extremes and rainfall variability, rice systems face increasing pressure to maintain productivity while reducing GHG emissions and improving resilience.

results.title: Comparing Measured Sonic Boom Turbulence-Induced Variability With Computational Models for the Carpet Determination in Entirety Measurements (CarpetDIEM) I Test Campaign
results.abstract: When a sonic boom propagates through the atmospheric boundary layer, atmospheric turbulence distorts the waveform, producing stochastic variations over short distances. Accurate prediction of this variability is essential because turbulence affects both waveform characteristics and human-perception metrics used to evaluate supersonic overflights. During NASA's 2019 Carpet Determination in Entirety Measurements I (CarpetDIEM I) flight test campaign, Brigham Young University deployed a 120 m (400 ft) linear array with seven microphones to quantify turbulence-induced variability of sonic boom waveforms, spectra, and metrics. In this study, state-of-the-art models PCBoom and KZKFourier are combined with two weather models, CFSv2 and ERA5, to predict metric variability and compare results with CarpetDIEM I measurements. Depending on the metric and confidence interval considered, prediction success ranges between about 30% and 80%. For the perceived level metric, the prediction successes for the mean and standard deviation were 30%–48% and 52%–65% respectively, depending on the weather model. This compares favorably with the Sonic Booms in Atmospheric Turbulence prediction success results of 45% and 71% for the perceived level mean and standard deviation respectively, using data reported by Stout, Sparrow, and Blanc-Benon [(2021). J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 149, 3250–3260].

results.title: Quantifying Methane Emissions from a Rich Fen with Uncrewed Aerial Systems in Boreal Alaska

organization.name: Alfred-Wegener-Institut Helmholtz-Zentrum für Polar- und Meeresforschung

results.abstract: Thawing of permafrost in northern latitudes is accelerating, potentially releasing significant amounts of methane (CH4) as forested permafrost plateaus transition into wetlands. This ecosystem shift alters the carbon exchange between the soil and atmosphere, influencing the permafrost-carbon feedback. Monitoring these changes requires measurement platforms operating across varied spatial and temporal scales. Recent advancements in Small Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (sUAS) enable high resolution CH4 flux quantification in remote, complex terrains, yet comparisons with established methods such as eddy covariance flux towers remain limited. In this study, we applied an airborne mass balance method using a hexacopter sUAS to quantify CH4 emissions from the Alaska Peatland Experiment, a wetland within the Bonanza Creek Experimental Forest. Using an ensemble of methods to define the background CH4 concentration, along with near surface emissions from soil chambers, helped constrain our flux estimates. The sUAS method yielded an average flux of 0.0077 ± 0.0019 mol s⁻¹ CH4, within a factor of two of concurrent tower-derived total source flux estimates (0.0036 ± 0.00042 mol s⁻¹ CH4). To assess spatial drivers of observed fluxes, we conducted a 2D footprint analysis and overlaid the results with high-resolution hyperspectral land cover classification, quantifying vegetative contributions within each footprint. This revealed higher fen representation in sUAS measurements (73.8%) than in tower footprints (58.8%), and lower tussock meadow representation (15.6% and 30.3%, respectively). These differences were consistent with known variation in vegetation-specific CH4 emissions. Our results highlight the importance of combining footprint modeling with land cover characterization to interpret airborne fluxes and guide cross-platform comparisons. To our knowledge, this is only the second sUAS-based CH4 flux study at the Bonanza Creek Experimental Forest, a rapidly changing boreal ecosystem.

results.title: Investigation of Bipropellant Plume-Induced Contamination Effects on Coverglass Materials
results.abstract:
Contamination and degradation of external spacecraft materials by unburned and partially combusted species from bipropellant thruster plumes has long been observed as a key component of the induced space environment. Space shuttle flight experiments and returned flight hardware from the International Space Station (ISS) have both experienced microscopic impact features induced by high-velocity thruster plume droplets. Analytical results have shown that droplet impingement angle relative to a receiving surface plays a key role in the surface damage. Although impacts with normal impingement angles contribute more severely to surface degradation than highly oblique angles, surface effects at higher impingement angles should not be dismissed.  

Thruster plume-induced materials degradation is a complex phenomenon that depends on a variety of parameters, including but not limited to material type, system temperature and pressure, plume composition, and thruster firing specifications such as number of pulses, pulse duration, and sample distance from the thruster. For space applications, attaining the vacuum pressure and temperature conditions necessary for flight-like plume expansion and exposure conditions is not a trivial task. The German Aerospace Center (Deutsches Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt, DLR) is a facility uniquely capable of simulating such conditions. 

Test coupons were exposed to bipropellant thruster firings under high vacuum at the DLR facility. Percent area coverage (PAC) and droplet size distributions were evaluated for the uncoated and coated solar array coverglass materials over a range of impingement angles (0̊ to 75̊). A post-test imaging workflow was developed that aimed to quantify changes in sample surface morphology obtained from scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images using the Image Processing and Analysis in Java (ImageJ) tool; an opensource image processing software. The goal was to create a framework through which to evaluate the effect of bipropellant-induced PAC and droplet size distribution on solar array coverglass optical transmission losses. Understanding this relationship is important because optical transmission losses are known to lead to current reduction in solar power generation systems.

In addition to the development of surface characterization workflows, valuable lessons learned as they pertain to future investigations and experiments will be discussed. The authors hope that sharing these lessons will facilitate more utilization of DLR’s unique capabilities as well as open the conversation for how best to address experimental characterization of flight-like plume expansion and its impacts on materials surface degradation effects.

results.title: Turbulence and its Potential Impact on Solar Chromospheric and Coronal Heating
results.abstract: Low-frequency turbulence in the solar chromosphere remains poorly understood. We address 1) the sources of low-frequency turbulence that potentially heat the chromosphere, and 2) how turbulence is transported and dissipated throughout the chromosphere and lower corona. We use particle-in-cell simulations to investigate mixed polarity magnetic fields corresponding to emergent magnetic carpet field in coronal holes or quiet Sun regions for strong (imbalanced) and weak (balanced) guide magnetic fields. The initial mixed polarity magnetic field transitions rapidly to a turbulent state dominated by advected small-scale nonlinear structures, with a minority slab turbulence population and the emergent field is largely annihilated. Turbulence is anisotropic for imbalanced magnetic field and more isotropic for balanced cases. We develop a transport model for turbulence advected and dissipated throughout the chromosphere by randomly distributed energy-containing scale dynamical flows described by log-normal statistics. We compute the expectations for the total energy per unit volume ⟨y⟩(h) J m−3, the Els ̈asser specific energy ⟨⟨Z∞2⟩⟩(h) m2 s−2, the heating rate ⟨  ̇H⟩(h) J m−3 s−1, and the correlation length ⟨λ⟩(h) km as functions of height h above the photosphere. Turbulent energy is injected into the low corona by a random “patchwork” of sites across the transition region surface. The expected energy injection rates ⟨  ̇S⟩ J m−2 s−1 for the chromosphere and at the base of the corona exceed the estimated energy requirements needed to heat both the chromosphere and corona. Similarly, we show that spicules can be heated gradually with increasing height by entrained magnetic carpet and photospheric turbulence.

results.abstract: The Caranca s meteorite is a H4-5 that exhibits extensive recrystallization of the matrix indicating metamorphism. Carancas contains dark, CI-like clasts that show no evidence of heating. Similar primitive xenolithic CI-like carbonaceous (C) clasts have also been observed in a range of other meteorites (ordinary chondrite, ureilite, howardite, and eucrite) [e.g., 2, 3]. Like other xenolithic clasts, the examined C clast of Carancas contains primitive organic matter (OM). However, in Carancas, this has also been observed to take the form of a vein-like structure. We investigated the organic and isotopic compositions of the OM-rich vein with Raman spectroscopy, X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), and NanoSIMS, to constrain its possible origin.

results.title: The Heterogenous Hydrogen Isotopic Composition of Bennu Samples

organization.name: Centre de Recherches Pétrographiques et Géochimiques
Centre de Recherches Pétrographiques et Géochimiques
Centre de Recherches Petrographiques et Geochimiques
Centre de Recherches Pétrographiques et Géochimiques

results.abstract:
Carbonaceous asteroids are potential contributors to water in the inner solar system and are likely to have contributed to the Earth's water budget. A fundamental tool that provides important constrains on the distribution of water reservoirs at the time of planetary formation is the hydrogen isotopic composition of primitive rocks derived from carbonaceous asteroids. However, only few primitive undifferentiated meteorites (chondrites) are avail-able for certain types of carbonaceous asteroids, and the potential of terrestrial contamination limits our ability to comprehend the distribution of water reservoirs in the protoplanetary disk from such materials.

On September 24, 2023, NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission delivered to Earth 121.6 g of fresh and pristine carbonaceous regolith from asteroid (101955) Bennu. The petrology of Bennu samples revealed that it the closest meteorite analogs are the chemically primitive chondrites, Ivuna-type carbonaceous chondrites (CIs), and the samples returned by the JAXA’s Hayabusa2 mission from the carbonaceous asteroid (162173) Ryugu. Bennu’s rock fragments underwent extensive aqueous alteration on the parent asteroid and are predominantly composed of hydrated sheet silicates (serpentine, smectite; ~80 vol.%) and other secondary minerals [1-2]. In order to obtain hints on the initial volatile-bearing constituents of Bennu’s parent asteroid (i.e., ices and organics), we have measured the D/H and C/H ratios in chondritic matrices by secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) in individual fine- to intermediate-sized particles of Bennu.

results.title: Bone Strength Assessment Using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) Compared to High-Resolution Peripheral QCT (HR-pQCT)

organization.name: Raymond and Ruth Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania
Hunter Holmes McGuire VA Medical Center

results.abstract:
Purpose: Accelerated bone strength loss is a hallmark of postmenopausal osteoporosis, spaceflight exposure, and disuse in conditions such as spinal cord injury. Three-dimensional imaging enables high-resolution characterization of bone microarchitecture, which can be used to construct finite element (FE) models for estimating mechanical strength and monitoring disease progression and treatment response. The objective of this study was to evaluate the accuracy of MRI-based FE analysis relative to high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT). 

Methods: Twenty-two subjects, including individuals with recent spinal cord injury (n=11) and abled-bodied controls (n=11), were recruited. Each subject underwent MRI on a Siemens MAGNETOM Vida system and Scanco HR-pQCT scanning of the left distal tibia. MRI parameters included 0.242 mm in-plane resolution, 1.5 mm slice thickness, TE/TR = 4.92/37 ms, field of view (FOV) = 124 mm, 18-channel body coil, and flip angle = 25° using a spoiled gradient echo (SPGR) sequence. HR-pQCT images were acquired using a standard 0.061 mm isotropic voxel size protocol. Both MRI and HR-pQCT datasets were converted into voxel-based FE meshes, and simulated compression was performed using a custom-built solver to estimate bone stiffness. 

Results: Distal tibia bone stiffness derived from MRI showed strong correlation with HR-pQCT-derived stiffness (R = 0.80). 

Conclusions: Despite substantial differences in imaging modality, spatial resolution, field of view, and contrast, MRI-derived bone stiffness demonstrated strong agreement with HR-pQCT estimates, even without image registration. MRI captured a broad spectrum of bone health (Figure 1). Given its ability to be performed on clinical MRI scanners using standard hardware and software at virtually any anatomical site and without ionizing radiation, MRI-based FE analysis offers a promising approach for assessing bone deterioration and monitoring treatment response at clinically critical fracture sites, such as the hip and spine. This is particularly valuable in populations including individuals with spinal cord injury, astronauts, and patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and chronic steroid use, in whom the utility of DXA remains limited or not well established.

results.title: Integrated Solar Panel Antenna Array for CubeSats (ISAAC)
results.abstract: This paper presents an integrated solar panel antenna array for CubeSats (ISAAC), which is an optically transparent reflectarray printed on the cover glass of a solar panel. The optical transparency of the antenna is 95% and with the 92% transparent cover glass, ISAAC has been measured to only reduce the efficiency of a triple junction solar cell from 29% (bare cell) to 24%. The antenna operates at 8.475 GHz, has a measured gain of higher than 21 dB after a full integration with the solar panel and after being conformal coated with Parylene HT for withstanding harsh elements. ISAAC is inkjet printed using conductive ink on a piece of 20 cm × 30 cm space certified glass. All components, from the antenna to solar panel, are commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS), space certified, and suitable a space deployment. Detailed analysis of different low-profile unit cells, loss due to conductive ink, effect of solar cells, and loss due to assembly are discussed, and methods to improve the antennas performance under these loss factors are presented.

results.abstract: CONVERGE links Venus exploration, planetary geoscience, terrestrial analogues, laboratory measurements, and rocky exoplanet studies. Within CONVERGE, we outline a Venus in-situ mission concept with three parts: an orbiter/relay, an analytical lander for a short surface stay, and a seismic/environmental station designed to last longer. The concept would add surface measurements at the same Venus site: mineral phases and bulk chemistry from a compact XRD/XRF instrument package, local imaging, near-surface atmospheric data, and passive seismic/environmental monitoring at a young volcanic rise such as Imdr Regio. These measurements would connect surface composition, alteration, and geophysical activity to orbital radar, spectroscopy, and atmospheric observations.

results.title: Anthropometric Human-Spacesuit Modeling Developments for Lunar Dynamic Loading Injury Scenarios
results.abstract: Lunar surface exploration will inherently expose humans to dynamic loading conditions in spacecraft and vehicles, where risk of injury can occur. In Lunar Terrain Vehicle (LTV) driving scenarios, the crewmember operates the vehicle while wearing a spacesuit, which increases the risk of blunt and repetitive contact injuries as the body collides with the internal components of the spacesuit. To assess injury risk, NASA uses Finite element (FE) human body models (HBMs) to derive injury metrics from dynamic loading forces/accelerations. It is important that astronaut anthropometry can be accurately represented in these models as injury mechanisms will change for different crewmember body shapes and sizes. At NASA, the Global Human Body Models Consortium (GHBMC) 5th percentile female, 50th percentile male, and 95th percentile male HBMs are used to assess dynamic loading. An anthropometric evaluation of these models indicates that they do not fully represent spacesuit anthropometric requirements. There are tools to adjust the body shape of HBMs such as the Position and Personalize Advanced Human Body Models for Injury Prediction (PIPER) software, but the default morphing pipeline is limited at representing subtle body shape morphology. Therefore, custom control point selection from 3D body scans and morphing algorithms are being systematically investigated to improve scaling of the GHBMC models. Initial results from a proof-of-concept example were encouraging as the morphed torso segments closely approximated the original scan data. Anthropometrically accurate HBMs will enable effective occupant protection injury assessments and inform key hardware designs in the context of crewmember safety.

results.title: Design and Optimization of an Open Rotor Stage
results.abstract: Open rotor propulsors enable greatly increased effective bypass ratios over current aircraft engines, resulting in significantly improved efficiencies. One of the most promising of these geometries is the “open fan”, which consists of a single rotor followed by a single stator. This configuration will be referred to as an “open rotor stage” for design work at NASA. In this work we consider the multidisciplinary design and optimization of an open rotor stage using a variety of 2D and 3D techniques. The 2D aerodynamic techniques used for design include a 2D Trefftz plane method, axisymmetric throughflow, and quasi-3D blade-to-blade CFD. Aerodynamic performance is prioritized, while structural requirements are met and some acoustic considerations are included. Between the rotor, stator, and hub profiles, a total of 101 design variables are used. Differences in the process of designing an open rotor stage vs. designing other high-speed propellers are also discussed. The current design, the NASA Optimized Propulsor for Efficiency and Noise (N-OPEN-1), achieves 84.7% net efficiency as predicted by 3D CFD, with further improvements expected to be possible. This design makes effective use of a slower rotor and a less tip-loaded work distribution than typical single-rotation propellers, allowing the stator to produce 14.8% of the thrust. Laminar flow on the blades was responsible for a 1.7% efficiency benefit and warrants further study.

results.title: Preliminary Dynamic Modeling of the Quarter-Scale Distributed Electric Propulsion Aircraft

organization.name: The University of Texas at El Paso

results.abstract: This paper describes the early-stage modeling of a quarter-scale distributed electric propulsion aircraft, based on the SUbsonic Single Aft eNgine (SUSAN) Electrofan, a transformative concept aircraft for which a model exists. The full-scale 180 passenger SUSAN concept has a single turbofan engine in the tail that both produces thrust and provides electrical power to 16 electric fans distributed across the wings utilizing a series/parallel hybrid architecture. The quarter-scale version would have an internal combustion piston engine to provide power to 17 electric fans–16 on the wings, one in the tail–in a series hybrid configuration, and no vertical or horizontal stabilizers. It would also have a reduced flight envelope in terms of both altitude and speed. The initial modeling approach is to scale down the original airframe model to capture the dynamic behavior of a much smaller aircraft,  albeit with an empennage. The original powertrain model is then replaced with one representing the physical components of that of the quarter-scale vehicle. This powertrain model is suitable for control design and analysis, and the fully integrated, although preliminary, aircraft model allows flight simulator testing and evaluation. Results from simulations are presented.

results.title: Prenatal Exposure to Prescribed Smoke PM2.5 and Low Birth Weight in Georgia, USA

organization.name: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

results.abstract: Background: Prescribed burning is a major but poorly characterized source of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) in the southeastern United States. While wildfire-related smoke PM2.5 has been linked to adverse birth outcomes, evidence on prescribed fire-related smoke (PFS) and birth weight remains limited, particularly in the Southeast. Objective: This study investigated the association between prenatal exposure to PFS-specific PM2.5 and birth weight in Georgia, USA. Methods: We analyzed 448,477 singleton term births (37–42 weeks of gestation) with last menstrual period (LMP) dates between January 1, 2013 and December 31, 2016. Daily ZIP code-level PFS PM2.5 concentrations were averaged over early gestation (first 4 and 6 weeks), each trimester, and the entire pregnancy. High-exposure metrics were defined as the number of days exceeding percentile-based thresholds for each exposure window. Linear regression models adjusted for non-PFS PM2.5, LMP date, gestational age, infant sex, and maternal characteristics. Results: Higher PFS PM2.5 exposure was independently associated with lower birth weight. Each 1 µg/m3 increase in average PFS PM2.5 during the first 4 weeks and the first trimester was associated with birth weight decreases of 3.22 g (95 % confidence interval [CI]: 0.82, 5.62) and 4.56 g (95 % CI: 0.12, 9.00), respectively. Each additional day exceeding the 95th percentile (1.21 µg/m3) of PFS PM2.5 during the entire gestation corresponded to an 11.70 g (95 % CI: 0.95, 22.45) reduction. Conclusion: Prenatal PFS exposure may reduce birth weight, particularly during early pregnancy, and both exposure intensity and duration are important in evaluating the health impacts of fire-related PM2.5.

results.title: Predicting Operational Performance of xEMU Boot at Lunar South Pole Temperatures using Thermal Desktop<sup>®</sup>

organization.name: HX5 (United States)
organization.location: Fort Walton Beach, Florida, United States

results.abstract: The spacesuit boots that will be used on Artemis lunar south pole surface missions will be exposed to extremely cold temperatures (down to ~50 K). To assess the performance of the government’s Exploration Extravehicular Mobility Unit (xEMU) lunar boot in these permanently shadowed regions, testing was performed at the Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) in the Cryogenic Ice Transfer, Acquisition Development, and Excavation Laboratory (CITADEL) thermal vacuum (TVAC) chamber. This paper documents the data analysis, thermal boot model correlation, and operational predictions conducted using data from the xEMU CITADEL TVAC test. Expected thermal conductances within the boot and between the boot and environment were calculated from test data, which was then used as an initial guess for conductances within a Thermal Desktop (TD) model. Correlation of the TD model using the internal SOLVER feature was performed across 10 different test points which varied external temperature, internal boot ventilation flowrate, and contact pressure. Operational performance at the lunar south pole was then predicted using results from the correlated model. While the predictions provide evidence for acceptable performance of the boots at the 100K environment test point, there is still substantial uncertainty in performance, especially at the 48K test point. This uncertainty is due in part to testing limitations such as contacting the foot to a hard metal plate rather than granular regolith, and model limitations such as the lack of a realistic foot model. These limitations and their impacts are addressed in detail in this paper. The results of this test series and model correlation underscore the importance of additional improved testing and modeling for characterizing the expected thermal resistance between the outside of the boot and the lunar surface.

results.title: Parametric-Based Heat Rejection Trade Study for Lunar and Martian Surface Operations

organization.name: HX5 (United States)
organization.location: Fort Walton Beach, Florida, United States

results.abstract:
Establishing and maintaining a sustained presence on the lunar and/or Martian surfaces will require a diverse portfolio of surface elements (e.g., habitation, mobility, power generation, etc.). Many of these systems generate excess heat that must be rejected across a wide range of magnitudes, temperatures, and duty cycles and under variable environmental conditions. To identify the most promising heat rejection approaches for this diverse portfolio, a heat rejection trade study was conducted to evaluate the performance of different technology approaches across a spectrum of surface environments and heat-load requirements. The trade study consisted of three stages: (1) development of a parametric-based modeling framework, (2) creation of a database of heat rejection technologies, surface elements, and environmental conditions for the Moon and Mars, and (3) execution of a quantitative analysis of various heat rejection technologies across different operating conditions and surface elements.

The modeling framework is developed in Python and Excel to prioritize small model size and hence low computational cost to enable large parametric sweeps while avoiding the reliance on proprietary software. Individual heat rejection processes are represented as simple Excel models, and a centralized Python script interfaces with the models to coordinate the  parametric study. These simple sizing models were developed to take heat load requirements and environmental parameters as inputs and compute mass, power, and volume as outputs. Rather than assess each heat rejection technology separately for each surface element, a unified parametric space was developed to evaluate all technologies across all elements. This parametric space includes factors related to heat load (e.g., magnitude or temperature) and environment (e.g., surface temperature, sky temperature, solar flux).

This effort generated a database containing information on over 60 heat rejection technologies and 30 surface elements. For each surface element, the expected heat rejection requirements were documented and analyzed to determine the most common needs shared across all elements. Environmental conditions at various lunar and Martian latitudes were also established for worst-case hot and worst-case cold scenarios.

High-fidelity heat rejection models are currently under development. Preliminary trades between heat rejection technologies including radiators, venting technologies, convective coolers, and more have been conducted to identify promising options. This presentation will summarize the preliminary trade results and provide an overview and discussion of the expected heat loads and thermal environments for sustained surface operations on the Moon and Mars.

results.title: Version 8 of the NASA SMAP Level 4 Soil Moisture Product
results.abstract: The NASA Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) mission Level 4 Soil Moisture (L4_SM) product provides global, 3-hourly, 9-km resolution soil moisture estimates with a mean latency of ~2.5 days from the time of observation.  The L4_SM estimates are derived through the assimilation of the brightness temperature (Tb) observations from the SMAP radiometer into the NASA Catchment land surface model.  The L4_SM assimilation system is based on a spatially distributed ensemble Kalman filter and produces optimal soil moisture estimates by considering the uncertainties in the land model estimates and the Tb observations.  Version 8 of the L4_SM product, first released in April 2025, features updated precipitation data used to drive the Catchment model and an improved version of the microwave radiative transfer model that links the simulated soil moisture and temperature estimates to the observed Tb.  Validation against in situ measurements from SMAP core validation sites indicates that the L4_SM Version 8 surface (root-zone) soil moisture estimates have an unbiased RMSE of 0.039 (0.026) m3 m-3, thereby meeting the SMAP mission accuracy requirement.  The typical magnitude of the Tb observation-minus-forecast differences in the L4_SM Version 8 product is 4.8 K, which represents an improvement of 0.2 K over the same metric for the Version 7 estimates.

results.title: A Gap and Impact Analysis for Surface Trajectory Based Operations (STBO) and Digital Taxi Clearances
results.abstract: Air travel has always had some inherent risk that cannot be engineered out, primarily in regard to how human beings operate within and outside the system. Surface Trajectory Based Operations (STBO) and Digital Taxi clearances help mitigate this risk by giving flight crews clearer instructions and a safer path forward when conducting the taxi phase of flight. However, cost remains a significant hurdle making adoption a daunting prospect, with new technologies requiring development, evaluation, and assurance. Analysis of voluntary reporting, accident reports, and the current structure of delays inside the NAS points to a gap in existing safety infrastructure that would benefit from the implementation of such advancements. While there are gains to be made from both a financial and efficiency perspective, there remains a significant barrier to entry that would require cooperation and commitment from operators, regulators, and manufacturers alike. This paper describes the current state of practice for surface safety, surveys existing literature on STBO and Digital Taxi, and estimates the cost and benefits associated with utilization of these technologies.
