results.title: Attenuating Thermal Transient Effects in Turbomachinery by Leveraging Ancillary Subsystems Part 1: Concept Description and Modeling
results.abstract: Gas turbine engines are integral to aviation, providing thrust for propulsion and power to support various aircraft systems needed to accomplish air vehicle missions. One challenge that aero engines face is a shift in operability due to thermal transients, which can alter component performance, reduce operability margins, and impact the rate of engine degradation. Potential for diminished operability must be accounted for in the engine design, leading to sacrificed performance. However, some ancillary subsystems being considered for future propulsion systems could provide opportunities to attenuate the effects of thermal transients. Here, methods for leveraging such ancillary systems to this end will be explored. Such attenuation will reduce variations in performance and operability while relaxing constraints that impact component design. Furthermore, it will enhance the impact of the ancillary systems and help justify their adoption. Three approaches are considered for the secondary use of thermal transient attenuation: (1) engine electrification, (2) intercooling, and (3) water injection. A modeling effort and simulation study has been executed to investigate potential impacts. Here, in Part 1 of this two-part report series, the focus is placed on presentation of background information, a description of the general concept, and the modeling approach. A preliminary simulation study is presented that supports the viability of the overarching concept of leveraging ancillary engine subsystems to mitigate adverse effects of thermal transients. The Part 2 report will present concept implementation details and transient simulation results along with discussion of the results and key takeaways.

results.title: Spacecraft Radiator Protection from Ionizing Radiation, Dust, and Excessive Heat Loss
results.abstract:
Under a Phase II SBIR project funded by NASA Johnson Space Center (Contract No. 80NSSC25C0088), Analytical Scientific Products LLC (ASP) has been developing an actively controlled louver to protect spacecraft radiators from degradation due to exposure to various types of environmental conditions. Of particular interest are ionizing radiation during spacecraft transit through the Van Allen belts, dust during spacecraft landing and surface operations on the moon, and excessive heat loss during the long lunar night especially near the poles where the local ambient temperatures can drop below -200°C. Exposure to ionizing radiation and dust can degrade the optical properties of the radiator coating that in turn reduces its ability to reject excess heat from the spacecraft into the environment. Exposure to the extremely low temperature conditions during the lunar night near the poles can freeze the radiator fluids that can compromise the integrity of the radiator. 

Passive louvers constructed using thick aluminum vanes are used currently to protect spacecraft radiators from some of the above effects, but they have several drawbacks: (i) their high aerial density makes it impractical to scale them to protect the much larger spacecraft radiators needed for future manned missions to the moon and beyond, (ii) the bimetallic actuators used to open and close the vanes in passive louvers rely on external temperature alone and so the louver cannot offer protection from dust and ionizing radiation when the ambient temperatures are high, and (iii) the bimetallic actuators need time scales of the order of hours to open and close.  

We have addressed the above limitations of passive louvers through the development of a low aerial density and rapidly actuating actively controlled louver. It is constructed from a custom alloy that offers much higher levels of protection against the ionizing radiation, dust and excessive heat loss at a fraction of weight compared to passive louvers while providing opening and closing time scales of the order of a second. Our modular design makes it easy to scale the system up or down depending on the application. We have recently constructed a 31 inch × 31 inch module of this louver and tested its functionality and effectiveness. These tests have shown that the louver can be opened and closed in less than 2 s. It reduces the transmission of ionizing radiation by 78% to 100% (depending on the radiation source), dust transmission by more than 93%, and heat loss by more than 97%. We are currently preparing to evaluate this device at the Johnson Space Center’s cryogenic vacuum chamber where it can be subjected to simulated lunar surface conditions. 

This paper provides a detailed discussion of the test designs as well as the data from tests that demonstrate the effectiveness in reducing the transmission of ionizing radiation, dust, and heat under laboratory conditions.

results.title: Development and Validation of a High-Vacuum Thermal Conductivity Testbed for Aerospace Interface Materials
results.abstract: Thermal Interface Materials (TIMs) are critical components in spacecraft thermal management systems, where thermal performance is strongly influenced by vacuum conditions, interface contact resistance, and layered metallic joint behavior. However, manufacturer-reported thermal conductivity values are often derived under idealized conditions and may not accurately represent performance within operational aerospace applications. To address this limitation, the Testbed for Advanced Interface Materials in Vacuum (TAIMV) was developed as a modular vacuum-compatible thermal conductivity characterization platform capable of evaluating aerospace-relevant TIM configurations under both ambient and high-vacuum environments. The testbed was derived from the ASTM C1044-16 guarded hot plate methodology and incorporates interchangeable layers of stainless steel coupon geometries, independently controlled main and guard heaters, embedded resistance temperature detectors (RTDs), thermocouples, multi-layer insulation (MLI), and a temperature-controlled cold plate to characterize through-thickness thermal gradients across layered interfaces. In the current configuration, interface compression is limited to the nominal contact pressure generated by the experimental stack assembly. Initial experimental campaigns were conducted at ambient pressure and below 1×10-5 torr for vacuum cases using multiple interface materials including Braycote 601EF and Krytox-based greases across a range of thermal operating conditions. In parallel, a coupled numerical Python thermal model was developed to predict temperature distribution throughout the stack while accounting for conduction, radiation, and parasitic heat transfer pathways and effective interface resistance effects. Experimental measurements and numerical predictions showed consistent thermal trends across multiple operating conditions and environmental states. Results also revealed measurable differences between ambient and vacuum thermal behavior, demonstrating the importance of interface resistance, parasitic heat transfer mechanisms, and stack geometry in determining effective thermal performance within layered thermal interfaces. The presented work establishes a foundation for future thermal model correlation efforts and expanded characterization of aerospace thermal interface materials under representative environmental conditions. Future work will focus on the integration of a load cell system to enable controlled pressure-dependent characterization of thermal interface materials under compressive loading. This capability will allow investigation of the influence of contact pressure on effective thermal conductivity, interface resistance, and thermal performance within layered aerospace thermal interfaces under representative operational conditions.

results.title: Coiled Resonators: Development of Theory and Comparison to Experimental Results
results.abstract: A common approach for sound-absorbing treatments takes the form of an orifice over a cavity. This approach, in the form of “perforate over honeycomb” is used for the mitigation of fan noise in jet engines as it combines acoustic performance with the ruggedness required for such an application. Conventional approaches require a substantial cavity depth to achieve effective absorption of low frequency sound. Alternative treatments to minimize the required volume of such acoustic treatments were examined, emphasizing the interaction between the orifice dimensions, cavity dimensions, and frequency. Expressions for acoustic resistance and reactance for an orifice over a cavity were calculated from a range of analytical expressions found in the literature, focusing on the no-flow condition with the direction of the incident sound wave normal to the surface of the acoustic liner prototypes. Using some of these expressions, prototypes of some of these absorbers were designed, constructed, and tested in the NASA Glenn Research Center Normal Incidence Impedance Tube.  Predicted values of resistance and reactance were compared to values calculated from the measurements.  Results indicated that further work is needed to understand the differences observed between the predicted and measured values of impedance for these models and prototypes which featured a perforated plate over either a straight or coiled channel.

results.title: Spaceflight Human Optimization and Performance: Positioning Astronauts in an Operational Framework to Promote Health, Fitness, and Mission Readiness

organization.name: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

results.abstract: Optimizing astronaut mission readiness is a multidisciplinary endeavor that should integrate concepts from aerospace medicine, human performance, sports science, nutrition, and engineering. Situating astronauts within a theoretical framework similar to that of operational athletes, while addressing top human systems capability needs outlined for future missions, may be optimal for promoting sustained health and performance before, during, and after missions to low-Earth orbit, the lunar surface, and Mars. Mission readiness can be optimized by enhancing physiological and behavioral/psychological performance through data-driven and individualized exercise countermeasures, health and performance monitoring, precision nutrition, and rehabilitation strategies. Appropriate and stable space food systems that facilitate adequate provision of nutrients and fluids to prime astronauts for mission-critical tasks and operational demands are needed, though research is needed into potential nutritional considerations that might be useful for future missions. Behavioral readiness programs should emphasize stress inoculation, adaptive decision-making, communication, Earth-independent operation functionality, conflict resolution, leadership, and team-based problem-solving before flight to promote healthy team dynamics in-flight, along with proper society reintegration and uptake of family and occupational roles post-flight. Exercise remains an essential countermeasure during spaceflight, with an emphasis on maximizing fitness before launch to mitigate in-flight declines and on maintaining fitness levels and functionality during flight through high-intensity multimodal exercise. Following return to Earth, rehabilitative programs serve to restore cardiovascular, sensorimotor, and skeletal function, followed by enhancing skill-based performance components through a phase-based training program. Continuous monitoring systems that provide insight into health, performance, sleep, cognitive, nutritional, and recovery status should enable data-driven decision-making on physical readiness across all mission phases. By integrating insight from multiple disciplines, this unifying approach delivers a theoretical framework for sustaining astronaut health and performance during extended-duration missions.

results.title: The Trajectory of Recent Solid State Fusion Results
results.abstract:
Both NASA and Google have explored and funded Low Energy Nuclear Reaction (LENR) aka Solid-State Fusion or Lattice Confinement Fusion (LCF) research.  NASA has funded efforts since 1989, and Google Research began in 2014. Google, and researchers initially-funded by Google, published significant scientific papers in Nature, Nature Communications and the Journal of Applied Physics.    

NASA began a significant set of LENR-triggering programs in 2012 resulting in papers in Physical Review C, the Journal of Electroanalytical Chemistry and the Journal of Condensed  Matter Nuclear Science.  Both NASA and Google engaged researchers across fields of nuclear physics, chemistry, electrochemistry, material science and more.  NASA built upon early novel gas pumping experiments then followed the patented work of the US Navy SPAWAR  (US8,419,919, “System and Method to Generate Particles”) and experiments with the Naval Surface Warfare  Centers.   Google supported researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL), the University of  British Columbia (UBC), MIT and others. This resulted in patent  applications and two granted patents (US10264661B2, “Target structure for enhanced electron screening” and  US10566094B2 “Enhanced electron screening through plasmon oscillations”).

These separate efforts, unknown to the researchers at the time, provided the impetus for the DoE ARPA-E LENR program followed by the DARPA DSO “Mechanisms for Amplification of Fusion Reaction Rates in Solids” (MARRS) program. This document briefly describes the overlapping NASA and Google Research efforts in plasma loading and electron screening emphasizing the results of the latest paper in Nature Communications.  The papers and patents cited are listed.

results.title: From Pretraining to Practice: Highlights From the 2026 ESA-NASA International Workshop on AI Foundation Models for Earth Observation

organization.name: IBM Research - Thomas J. Watson Research Center

results.abstract:
The second ESA-NASA International Workshop on AI Foundation Models for Earth Observation brought together the Earth observation and AI communities from academic, commercial, and governmental organizations to assess the rapidly evolving role of foundation models in geospatial science applications. Hosted by NASA Marshall Space Flight Center in May of 2026, the workshop built on the inaugural meeting by shifting focus from early alignment and prototyping toward how geospatial foundation models should be pretrained, evaluated, adapted, trusted, deployed, and governed.

Across the workshop, a clear theme emerged: the community has moved beyond questioning whether large models can be pretrained on satellite data. Instead, discussions centered on what pretraining should teach, what information current models fail to capture, how model outputs can be trusted, and when foundation model approaches provide practical value over conventional methods. During sessions, attendees repeatedly emphasized that no single pretraining recipe, model architecture, benchmark, or deployment strategy fits all downstream tasks, making data quality, curation, uncertainty, evaluation design, operational constraints, and user-centered validation just as critical to scale. 

The workshop also highlighted a transition from standalone foundation models toward broader geospatial AI systems. Open-source tools, scalable serving approaches, embedding products, onboard inference, operational decision-support applications, and agentic AI workflows are beginning to connect these models with data archives, benchmarks, scientific literature, code, and human expertise. This report summarizes pivotal discussions from the workshop and outlines future directions for benchmarking, embeddings, adaptation, operationalization, trust, agentic AI, and the unique role of public agencies in supporting an open, reliable geospatial AI ecosystem.

results.title: Euhabitability: A New Term to Aid in the Search for Life in Addition to the Habitable Zone Framework

organization.name: Blue Marble Space Institute of Science
Deutsches Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt e. V. (DLR)

sourceIdentifiers.descriptor: This article is included in the The Geoscience of Exoplanets: Going Beyond Habitability collection.

results.abstract: The search for life on exoplanets is difficult due to observational limitations stemming from vast separating distances. The Habitable Zone (HZ) is a simplifying framework for identifying exoplanets that may be suitable for life, given our observational limitations. The HZ framework is built on many simplifying assumptions and only attempts to bound the circumstellar regions where surface oceans are not precluded. In other words, HZ exoplanets are where surface oceans are possible, not necessarily where life is possible. Water is essential for life as we know it, however, life requires additional factors such as nutrients and a magnetosphere. Therefore, the criteria of the HZ framework is one step removed from assessing the suitability for life. This nuance is easily lost in translation and has caused confusion among researchers and the general public; as the term “Habitable Zone” implies that planets in the HZ are habitable and those outside are uninhabitable. Here we define a new term, euhabitable (suitable for life), that addresses this confusion. In brief, a euhabitable exoplanet can exist outside the HZ (e.g., a Europa-like planet), and an uninhabitable exoplanet can exist within the HZ (e.g., a desiccated planet). The “euhabitable” term can be used to discuss these cases explicitly, avoiding confusion between an exoplanet’s suitability for life and it’s position relative to the HZ. The euhabitable framework is informed by the advancements in astrobiology over the past three decades, and primes exoplanet science for the future by moving the habitability discussion beyond “follow the water.”

results.title: Unified Radiative Transfer Model Supporting Cross-Spectrum Cross-Domain Applications
results.abstract:
Radiative Transfer Models (RTMs) are the foundation of modern Earth science applications, driving advancements in remote sensing, numerical weather prediction, climate modeling, and AI-driven analytics. However, the scientific community urgently needs a unified RTM framework based on consistent physical models across the electromagnetic spectrum (microwave to ultraviolet) for both atmosphere-land and atmosphere-ocean systems. A unified RTM would enable the synergistic use of disparate satellite datasets to ensure consistency and continuity, maximize information content, and expedite algorithm development for future missions.

To address this need, we propose establishing a dedicated, sustainably funded Radiative Transfer Modeling Working Group (RTMWG). By uniting cross-disciplinary expertise, the RTMWG will guide the selection of standardized spectroscopic and scattering data to build a modular, version-controlled, and open-source RTM. Through this collaborative framework, a state-of-the-art, physically consistent model can be delivered within a few years. Ultimately, this open-source RTM will serve as a reliable, easily updatable foundation for next-generation satellite remote sensing, sensor design trade study, satellite inter-calibration, numerical weather prediction (NWP) data assimilation, and climate modeling. The RTMWG will also engage closely with end-user communities to ensure long-term maintenance and support for the resulting databases, tools, and code.

results.title: Tracing the Source of Carbon Oxides on the Large Moons of Uranus

organization.name: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory

results.abstract: The Uranian moons Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon are enriched in CO<sub>2</sub> mixed with CO, but the origin(s) of these carbon oxides, be they primarily native or radiolytic, remain(s) uncertain. Using data collected by NIRSpec on the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), we measured the spectral signature of CO<sub>2</sub> and other carbon oxides to help disentangle these hypotheses. Through comparison to laboratory data, we find that many of the detected spectral features are consistent with CO<sub>2</sub> ice, including <sup>12</sup>CO2 scattering peaks (4.15–4.26 μm), multilobe <sup>13</sup>CO<sub>2</sub> bands (4.35–4.43 μm), and CO<sub>2</sub> biphonon and triphonon modes (4.80–5.25 μm). Our measurements show that CO<sub>2</sub> and CO are concentrated on the trailing hemispheres of the inner moons Ariel and Umbriel, potentially supporting a radiolytic production hypothesis, consistent with prior ground-based results. However, many of the identified spectral features are only observed in thick crystalline ice deposits measured in the laboratory, which may be difficult to form via radiolysis of carbon-bearing material mixed in icy regoliths. Similarly, the data exhibit weak 4.02 and 4.40 μm bands, hinting at the presence of carbonate minerals and <sup>13</sup>CO<sub>2</sub> clathrates, respectively, possibly formed in the interiors of these moons. Furthermore, JWST has revealed that CO<sub>2</sub> is widespread at Uranus, present in its system of rings, ring moons, and irregular satellites, consistent with its largest moons accreting CO<sub>2</sub> and other carbon oxides from the Uranian subnebula. We conclude that exposed carbon oxides are potentially native, with their surface distributions shaped by charged particle irradiation and seasonal sublimation–condensation cycles.

results.title: Hyperspectral Detail Meets Radiometric Accuracy: A Foundational Reflected Solar Capability for the Coming Decade

organization.name: Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics

results.abstract: Hyperspectral Earth-reflected solar measurements contain rich, detailed information about clouds, aerosols, and the atmosphere. This information compounds when paired with high, SI-traceable radiometric accuracy. Unlike spectral resolution, which can be resampled to coarser spectral resolutions, radiometric accuracy cannot be recovered once a measurement is made, making the choice to invest in this capability now a decision with lasting consequences for the climate record. CLARREO Pathfinder is demonstrating that this combination of hyperspectral sampling and benchmark-quality accuracy is achievable today, but no follow-on mission is currently planned within NASA's Earth Science Division portfolio, and the recent cancellation of the European Space Agency TRUTHS mission has heightened the urgency of sustaining this capability. We recommend prioritizing investment in a follow-on to CLARREO Pathfinder, along with dedicated support for the science community to fully exploit these measurements. This capability would reduce long-standing uncertainties in cloud feedback, aerosol forcing, and global energy imbalance, while providing a degradation-resistant, gap-resilient calibration foundation for the broader Earth observing system. Building on flight-proven technology and an engaged science community, this is a near-term, fiscally realistic opportunity to secure a foundational Earth observation capability for the coming decade.

results.title: RApid Blade-Vortex Interaction Tool (RABIT) User’s Manual - Version 1.0

organization.name: Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, New York

results.abstract: Identifying and reducing rotorcraft noise is essential to urban air mobility (UAM). Blade-vortex interaction (BVI) can be a major contributor to rotary-wing vehicle noise, particularly during flight phases where a close and nearly parallel interaction occurs between a rotor blade and a strong tip vortex. These interactions often happen during the descent and landing phases of flight when the vehicle is near the ground and therefore, near people. Reducing public noise exposure requires fast BVI estimations to rapidly assess the acoustic signature of rotary-wing vehicles. The RApid Blade-Interaction Tool (RABIT) is a fast, user-friendly, stand-alone computer program/application that predicts BVI strength and location using a prescribed wake model and a simple blade motion model. It also determines blade and wake intersection timing and location and provides visualizations to support conceptual design, rotor placement, and rotor-wake interaction assessments. This manual outlines the background of the RABIT tool, theory, validation cases, installation process, interface, output files, and example applications.

results.title: NASA Engineering and Safety Center Technical Bulletin No. 26-07: Aluminum Alloy 2219 Material Guidance
results.abstract:
Improper casting and forging processes in the manufacture of aluminum alloy 2219 can lead to microstructural defects that result in a sub-optimal response to anodic surface treatments and an increase in corrosion susceptibility. This Technical Bulletin communicates the risks of improper casting and recommends a homogenizing step followed by multidirectional deformation after conventional direct
chill casting, especially for larger castings.

results.title: Analysis of Single and Contra-Rotating Propellers
results.abstract:
The high efficiency of open rotor propulsion is attractive to designers of sustainable transport aircraft configurations of the future. Modern open rotors for transonic aircraft are geometrically complex, can involve multiple stages (e.g. downstream stator or contra rotating second rotor) and typically operate under conditions where the flow over a portion of the blade is transonic. The overall net efficiency of modern open rotors can approach 86% at a cruise Mach number of 0.8 leading to significant fuel savings in comparison to turbofan engines. Modern open rotors are considerably quieter than the propfans of the 1980s.

Modeling of open rotor configurations to predict the thrust produced and power required is believed by many to be outside the capabilities of traditional blade element analysis but this may be because of blade geometrical and aerodynamic modeling deficiencies not an inherent deficiency in the blade element approach. Presented in this memorandum is a description of the modeling approach behind a newly developed Blade Element Momentum Theory analysis code called PyRotor that is written in the Python programming language. The underlining theory and functionality of the code are described. Several rotors, ranging in complexity from a simple two-blade propeller up to a modern CR rotor system, are analyzed and compare favorably with previously published measured data.

results.abstract: LiteBIRD is a JAXA-led space mission designed to produce all-sky microwave polarization maps. Its primary science goal is to test representative inflationary models by measuring the cosmic microwave background B-mode polarization generated by primordial gravitational waves, while also providing new insights into cosmology, particle physics, and astrophysics. The mission concept has been updated following the reformation activities initiated after the Mission Definition Review in 2024. The current concept preserves the central scientific objectives, while simplifying the payload configuration: a single telescope covers 12 frequency bands with band centers spanning 40 to 402 GHz, corresponding to an optical coverage of 34–448 GHz. The telescope is a cross-Dragone reflector with a 500-mm aperture diameter, cooled to approximately 5 K and coupled to transition-edge-sensor bolometer arrays operated at 0.1 K. LiteBIRD will observe from a Lissajous orbit around the Sun–Earth L2 point during a nominal 3-year survey. More specifically, the primary scientific objective is to achieve total uncertainty in the tensor-to-scalar ratio of δr < 0.002 (68% C.L.), including contributions from foreground residuals, statistical uncertainties, instrumental systematics, and margin contingency. The corresponding map-noise requirements are specified separately for the low-, mid-, and high-frequency ranges over the reionization and recombination multipole ranges. This sensitivity makes LiteBIRD unique not only for inflationary science but also for a broad range of scientific investigations probing the history of both the early and late Universe, as well as for astrophysical processes, including Galactic science. This paper summarizes the scientific objectives, updated payload and instrument concepts, observation strategy, and ground segment plans.

organization.name: NRC Herzberg Astronomy and Astrophysics Research Centre

results.abstract: The Canadian Galactic Emission Mapper (CGEM) radio telescope is mapping polarized Galactic foregrounds from 8-10 GHz to aid in the search for B-modes in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). Here we describe the design and early on-sky characterization of the CGEM optics. CGEM employs an on-axis, hat feed optical design that is a body of revolution (BOR) and exhibits excellent intrinsic polarization purity. We describe how we have optimized the optics with a novel framework that can directly minimize simulated intensity to polarized intensity (T → P) leakage in angular power spectrum space. The optimized optics exhibit simulated T → P leakage that is orders of magnitude below anticipated CℓBB for r = 10<sup>−3</sup> when scaled from 8-10 GHz to the CMB observing window near 95 GHz. We go on to describe the mechanical design of the optics, including a novel secondary mirror support made from Astroquartz composite that has low loss, low dielectric constant, and preserves the BOR symmetry of the optics. We then showcase the early on-sky performance of the optics with observations of the Sun and satellites, which probe the beam to 40dB down from the peak. A beam model for the deployed CGEM optics based on electromagnetic simulations is in excellent agreement with the on-sky data.

results.title: Lunar Dust Vacuum Cleaner Status Report
results.abstract: This report documents the development, execution, and analysis of a lunar dust vacuum cleaner test campaign performed to better understand particulate removal from space suit materials in support of future Artemis missions. The work includes fabrication of representative Ortho fabric test coupons, controlled loading of lunar simulants using a repeatable simulant loading device, and vacuum-based particulate removal testing under defined flow and contamination conditions. Multiple sources of uncertainty associated with sample preparation, simulant distribution, penetration depth, adhesion, cohesion, and vacuuming parameters were identified and mitigated through refined procedures and measurement techniques. Post-test analysis relied primarily on high-precision mass measurements, supplemented by microscopy assessments to characterize particle distribution and limitations of available analytical tools. A predictive particle resuspension model based on the Reeks and Hall “Rock’n’Roll” framework was implemented to complement experimental results, including verification against published data and evaluation of parameter sensitivity. Together, the experimental and modeling outcomes provide insight into removal efficiency trends, repeatability improvements, and the influence of contamination and flow variables. These results inform recommendations for future testing, operational considerations, and vacuum system design for effective lunar dust management.

results.stiTypeDetails: Other - Results for ASTM round robin activity on the sandwich mixed-mode bend test
results.abstract:
The results provided within this spreadsheet are for an American Society for Testing and 
Materials (ASTM) International round robin on the sandwich mixed-mode bend (S-MMB) 
test, which was conducted in June and July of 2026 at the NASA Langley Research 
Center. The S-MMB test is designed to measure fracture toughness corresponding to 
mixed mode-I/II facesheet/core disbonding in a sandwich composite. The S-MMB test 
fixture is depicted in Figure 1 with an S-MMB specimen positioned in the fixture. The S
MMB test is the superposition of a flexure test and a tensile test to result in mixed mode
I/II loading at the facesheet/core disbond front of an S-MMB specimen. Three different 
mode ratios were evaluated, namely 0.18GII/GT, 0.35GII/GT, and 0.51GII/GT, where GII 
is the mode II fracture toughness and GT is the total fracture toughness, and four tests 
were performed at each mode ratio.  Prior to testing S-MMB specimens were pre-cracked 
using the S-MMB test fixture with a lever arm length of 305 mm, resulting in an 
approximately 20-mm-long facesheet/core disbond. Lever arm length and the location of 
the resulting facesheet/core disbond are illustrated in Figure 1. Each S-MMB specimen 
was loaded in stroke control at the location indicated in Figure 1.  Load was measured 
using a 2.5 kN (550 lbf) load cell and the stroke was measured using the internal linear 
variable displacement transducer of the test machine used to conduct the S-MMB tests. 
The test fixture and specimen were aligned prior to testing using shims. Both specimen 
edges were painted white over which markers were added to highlight disbond growth 
during a test. Two cameras, each facing one edge of a specimen, were used to take 
images during testing at a 1.0Hz sample rate. 

The material system evaluated in this study is a sandwich composite consisting of a 
carbon/epoxy facesheet with a foam internal core. The carbon/epoxy facesheet is made 
from Solvay CYCOM 5276-1 G30-500PW prepreg and has the layup configuration of 
[45/0/0/45]s and were cured used using the manufacturer’s recommended cure cycle. 
The thickness of the facesheet is approximately 1.6 mm, with an average ply thickness 
of 0.2 mm. The core used in this study is a Rohacell 61 HERO polymethacrylimide (PMI) 
foam with a core density of 75 kg/m3 and a thickness of 19.05 mm. The length and width 
of each specimen are 304.8 mm and 50.1 mm, respectively. The specimens were stored 
in a desiccator in a laboratory, room-temperature environment prior to testing. During 
loading, the samples subjected to an applied displacement at a rate of 5mm/min.

results.title: Direct Radiative Impacts of Stratospheric Aerosols on the Tropical Troposphere: Clouds, Precipitation, and Circulation in Convection-Resolving and Global Simulations
results.abstract: A concern for stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) is that stratospheric aerosols could inadvertently alter rain and winds through mechanisms independent of the intended surface cooling. Here, we investigate how the tropical troposphere responds to SAI in models of different complexity, including convection-resolving mock-Walker and small-domain simulations as well as a global climate model, with sea surface temperature held fixed. Across models, we trace the mechanisms driving tropospheric impacts and identify modeling limitations that hinder accurate risk evaluation. SAI enhances downward longwave radiation from the warmed, aerosol-rich stratosphere, generating upper-tropospheric radiative heating that reduces cloudiness and suppresses convection, reducing precipitation. While our best estimate is a ∼2% tropical-mean precipitation reduction under strong SAI at fixed sea surface temperature, this is counteracted by cloud radiative responses that hinder predictability. Further, sensitivity experiments suggest that the precipitation response may hinge on how SAI is enacted, with higher and smaller particles both tending to weaken the precipitation response, in partial agreement with prior findings. Our convection-resolving simulations do not show that surface-temperature-independent effects of stratospheric aerosols inherently weaken the tropical overturning circulation, as previously suggested. While regional precipitation responses within the tropics could be substantial, our simulations suggest potential for lower risks than analogous volcanic events by releasing aerosols gradually, thereby mitigating land–sea circulation responses. These results clarify the mechanisms governing SAI hydroclimate impacts and reveal limitations affecting simulated outcomes from contemporary models. Consequently, near-term SAI deployment would carry the risk of being implemented without the ability to reliably predict its hydroclimate impacts.

results.title: In-Situ Resource Utilization Using Drilling Regolith for Excavation and Analysis of Moon Surface (DREAMS) Hopper for Self-Sustaining Lunar Habitat

organization.name: Texas Academy of Math and Science at the University of North Texas

results.abstract: Over 50 years ago, NASA’s Apollo missions answered many of humanity’s questions from space to biosciences while advancing computing capabilities. Orbital spacecraft and rovers have transformed our understanding of the moon. Recently, the completion of Artemis II has initiated a new era focused on sustained lunar presence and autonomous exploration. However, a gap remains between scientific resource characterization and technology required for long-term exploration utilizing these resources. For these reasons, we propose a framework comprising of three complementary systems: the Drilling Regolith for Excavation and Analysis of Moon Surface (DREAMS) hopper, the Terrain-adaptive Regolith Excavator (T-REx) rover, and the MoonFall drones. DREAMS identifies and characterizes resource-rich regolith deposits through subsurface drilling and sampling, while T-REx autonomously excavates and transports regolith to a lunar base for further processing. The MoonFall drones aid T-REx with path planning and navigation on the lunar surface. At the base, 3D printers use processed regolith to manufacture components necessary to support sustained surface operations while reducing dependence on earth-supplied materials. Within this framework, these systems provide an operational concept for exploring permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) near the lunar south pole while collecting geological and engineering data through regolith extraction. Through systems engineering analysis, we evaluated the feasibility of integrating drilling, excavation, regolith transport, and additive manufacturing into an in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) architecture while considering the scientific and engineering objectives of this operational concept. Ultimately, Project DREAMS demonstrates an approach to sustainable lunar exploration while simultaneously establishing a foundation for future deep-space human missions.

results.title: Weak Lensing Mass Calibration of the ACT DR5 Galaxy Clusters with the DES Year 3 Weak Lensing Data

organization.name: Kavli Institute for Particle Astrophysics and Cosmology

results.abstract: We use weak gravitational lensing measurements from Year 3 Dark Energy Survey data to calibrate the masses of 443 galaxy clusters selected via the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect from Atacama Cosmology Telescope Data Release 5 maps of the cosmic microwave background. We incorporate redshift and SZ measurements for individual clusters into a hierarchical model for the stacked lensing signals and perform Bayesian analyses to constrain the hydrostatic mass bias of the clusters. Our treatment of systematic uncertainties includes a prescription for measuring and accounting for the weak lensing boost factor, consideration of a miscentering effect, as well as marginalization over uncertainties in the source galaxy photometric redshift distributions and shear calibration. The resultant constraints on the normalization of the mass-observable relation have a precision of approximately 7%, with the mean WL halo mass of M<sub>500c</sub> = 5.4 × 10<sup>14</sup>M⊙. We measure the bias between the true cluster mass and the mass estimated from the SZ signal based on an X-ray–calibrated scaling relation assuming hydrostatic equilibrium, to be 1 - b = 0.74<sup>+0.06</sup><sub style='position: relative; left: -2.5em;'>−0.05</sub> over the full sample. When splitting the clusters into high (z = 0.43–0.70) and low (z = 0.15–0.43) redshift bins, we measure 1 - b = 0.58<sup>+0.06</sup><sub style='position: relative; left: -2.5em;'>−0.05</sub> and 0.81<sup>+0.08</sup><sub style='position: relative; left: -2.5em;'>−0.06</sub>, respectively. When introducing additional freedom in redshift and mass to the hydrostatic bias model, we find that 1 - b decreases with redshift (with the power law of -1.8<sup>+0.06</sup><sub style='position: relative; left: -2.5em;'>−0.05</sub>, 99.95% confidence), consistent with findings from other recent studies, while we do not find any significant trend in mass. We also demonstrate that our result is robust against various systematics such as a scale cut, priors on baryonic and miscentering parameters, and degree of scatter in mass-observable relation. The weak-lensing mass calibration presented in this study will be a useful tool for using the ACT clusters as probes of astrophysics, and as a step towards using their abundance as a cosmological probe.

results.title: What the Solar System Can Teach Us About Rocky Exoplanets
results.abstract: The number of rocky extrasolar planets being discovered continues to increase, but so too does the apparent diversity of such worlds. As we work to understand the likely bulk properties and thermal, geological, and climatological attributes we might expect of rocky exoplanets, we can look to the Solar System for guidance. Here, we review the interior, surface, and atmospheric characteristics of modern Earth, and discuss how our homeworld has changed through Solar System history. We then visit in turn Venus, Mars, Mercury and Earth’s Moon, and Io, noting how these terrestrial planets are alike, how they are different, and how they have evolved through time. Finally, we consider some examples of the types of rocky worlds known or suspected to exist without direct Solar System counterparts—but we argue that even then, for all the variety we might expect, they are still variations on a common theme. Perhaps the most important lesson the Solar System can teach us is that terrestrial bodies change through time, sometimes dramatically, and that rocky worlds of similar size and mass can have vastly different planetary outcomes.

results.title: The Cloud Feedback Model Intercomparison Project (CFMIP) contribution to CMIP7
results.abstract: Cloud processes constitute one of the key uncertainties for climate change projections. The fourth iteration of the Cloud Feedback Model Intercomparison Project, CFMIP4, contributes to the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 7 (CMIP7), by providing a set of global climate model experiments aiming to enhance our understanding of clouds, circulation and climate sensitivity, thereby informing improved projections of future climate change. CFMIP4 targets four knowledge gaps: (1) Physical mechanisms of cloud feedback and adjustment; (2) Dependence of cloud feedback and adjustment on climate base state and on the nature of the forcing; (3) Coupled mechanisms of the sea-surface temperature “pattern effect”; and (4) Coupling of clouds with circulation and precipitation. CFMIP4 contributes four CMIP7 Assessment Fast Track experiments that are central to the quantification of climate feedback and sensitivity in past, present and future climates, essential for process understanding and model evaluation. Furthermore, CFMIP4 supports the joint analysis of models and observations through a data request that includes process and satellite simulator output.

results.title: Nanofibrillated Cellulose-Regolith Composite Aerogels for Lunar Thermal Insulation
results.abstract: Life support systems in extraterrestrial settings face severe material constraints, demanding innovative in situ resource utilization (ISRU) strategies. One material that merits attention is cellulose, which can be procured in relative abundance from locally generated waste. Here, we present an ISRU approach toward thermally insulating composite aerogels based on nanofibrillated cellulose (NFC) and a lunar regolith simulant. Cellulose fibers are ground by planetary ball milling with lunar highland simulant (LHS-1) into NFC-regolith slurries with subsequent conversion into aerogels by supercritical drying. Comminution of cellulose fibers and LHS-1 particles enable the production of composite aerogels with thermal conductivities as low as 30 mW/m·K. Multiparametric optimization of aerogel properties can be guided by design of experiments (DOE) based on the mass ratios of NFC in water, LHS-1 in aerogel, and amount of milling media. The study illustrates how composite aerogels made of regolith and fibrillated cellulose can provide sustainable routes toward functional materials for lunar habitats and other extraterrestrial resource-limited environments.

results.abstract: Accurate simulation of crop evapotranspiration (ET) is critical for water management and for understanding the impacts of climate variability and change. Yet evidence on model skill in simulating ET remains limited, and the sources of error remain poorly understood. Daily simulations from 17 wheat crop models were evaluated against field observations from two sites in semi-arid and Mediterranean environments under water-limited and irrigated conditions. Absolute ET errors were larger under irrigation, but this contrast was substantially attenuated after normalization by observed ET. The larger absolute errors under irrigation were mainly associated with a greater lack-of-correlation component rather than stronger systematic bias, indicating greater day-to-day mismatch between simulations and observations. Differences among ET-demand approaches also tended to be more evident under irrigation, with Priestley–Taylor-based models tending to produce larger errors, although the broad method classes also differed in other model components. Mixed-effects attribution showed that the conditional associations between ET error and climatic factors differed between the two water-supply datasets. Under irrigation, ET simulation error was associated with vapour pressure deficit (VPD), wind speed, radiation, and the component of maximum temperature not linearly explained by VPD, whereas under water-limited conditions meteorological attribution was weaker and observed soil–water status provided additional information. Root-zone soil moisture provided greater model support than shallow or deep soil moisture and modified the association between VPD and ET error. These findings identify atmospheric-demand representation and root-zone water availability as priorities for improving the evaluation and development of crop ET simulations.

results.title: What Does Sensor Performance Really Mean? A Four-Layer Framework for Interpreting Air Quality Sensor Performance Evaluations

organization.name: C40 Cities Climate Leadership Group Inc

results.abstract: Air quality (AQ) sensors are increasingly used to complement sparse reference-grade monitoring networks, enabling denser spatial coverage, rapid deployment, and new monitoring approaches. Yet sensor performance evaluations (SPEs) are often communicated through headline metrics and comparative benchmarks that may obscure how results were produced and what they can legitimately support. Under real-world decision constraints, such results may be treated as decision-ready evidence even when their underlying basis remains incomplete. Here we propose a four-layer framework for interpreting SPE claims for fixed outdoor AQ sensors. The framework is organized around four main questions: who led the evaluation, what data product was actually evaluated, under what context it was evaluated, and what the reported metrics do (and do not) convey. From these, we derive a set of guiding questions to help users identify what information is available, missing, or uncertain, avoid over-interpreting underdescribed results, and make more grounded comparisons across studies and sources. The framework is not intended to determine fitness-for-purpose or prescribe a decision. Rather, it helps end users make the evidential basis of a performance claim more explicit so they can decide what information matters for their particular use case and whether further clarification or evidence is needed.

results.title: Assurance, Verification and Validation of Routine Autonomous Multi-Aircraft Operations
results.abstract: Effective assurance, verification and validation (V&V) methods will be necessary to enable certification of routine autonomous multiple aircraft operations (RAMAO). Unfortunately, the complexity of these systems, diversity of market, airspace integration and differing rates of technological change make assurance of these operations challenging. A traditional approach to this assurance problem is to handle one incremental change at a time in the following cycle: 1) Develop incremental technology using a V&V amenable design life cycle, 2) Work with regulators to generate prescriptive certification approach, and 3) Certify and deploy incremental technology. While such an approach has proved successful in developing many safe and reliable systems, it would be slow and cumbersome applied to the RAMAO domain as each piece of technology would have to be matured and frozen before adding the next piece. In addition, a traditional approach would create a patchwork of bespoke certification frameworks for a large number of systems making it difficult to reuse prior certification pathways. Therefore, this white paper argues that we need a more dynamic approach for assurance for the RAMAO domain. This dynamic process involves an objective certification approach where certification is based on the needs of a particular system. Then to satisfy the approach, a safety case is made where safety arguments are made followed by V&V evidence supporting this safety case. We believe this structure is flexible enough to allow for assurance of more dynamic domains while also allowing a mix of more traditional assurance approaches where appropriate.

results.title: Future of Hygiene: Systems, Signals, and Scenarios
results.abstract:
Hygiene is a foundational but often invisible system. It is both highly personal and deeply infrastructural. Long treated as a matter of individual responsibility, hygiene reveals how societies distribute resources, manage risk, and assign value. It affects not just physical health, but emotional regulation, social participation, and environmental stability.

Today, hygiene systems face mounting pressure from climate volatility, water scarcity, aging populations, antimicrobial resistance, and growing sensory and neurodiverse needs. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is already a global health crisis, contributing to an estimated 1.14 million deaths in 2021 alone, with projections suggesting up to 39 million deaths worldwide between 2025 and 2050 if current hygiene, sanitation, and antimicrobial practices remain unchanged (Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, 2022). At the same time, new technologies are reshaping hygiene, from smart surfaces and data-driven cleaning systems to AI-enabled hygiene coaching and predictive diagnostics. These shifts present critical questions: Who is hygiene for? Who decides what is “clean”? And what values do our hygiene systems reflect?

This project explores hygiene as a lens for long-term systems transformation. Through interviews, signal analysis, and strategic foresight methods, we identify the assumptions embedded in current hygiene systems and examine how they may evolve over the coming decades. The report presents four futures set in the year 2055, each illustrating different trajectories of change, including infrastructural collapse and ecological realignment. The scenarios are not predictions. They are tools to help decision-makers explore tradeoffs, imagine alternatives, and surface new questions about hygiene and public infrastructure. Alongside these scenarios, the report identifies four strategic priorities for future hygiene systems: investing in resilient and distributed infrastructure,
protecting access to hygiene as a public good, redesigning hygiene governance to center dignity over control, and aligning technology with lived emotional and environmental realities. 

Hygiene is not simply about eliminating germs. It is about how people manage their bodies in relation to environments, norms, and systems. When designed with care, hygiene becomes an infrastructure of safety, trust, and adaptive response. In a world defined by disruption, investing in resilient hygiene systems is not just a public health strategy. It is a commitment to future readiness.

results.title: Origin of low ozone above western North America: an investigation of sources and trends

organization.name: Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences

results.abstract: While free-tropospheric ozone (O3) over western North America (WNA) has increased since the mid-1990s, research has primarily focused on the mean. We investigate the lower tail (O3 < 33rd percentile) to characterize the evolving remote background state. Because these air masses are minimally affected by episodic extremes, they offer a clearer window into long-term shifts in background O3, transport, and photochemistry. Using FLEXPART-ERA5 source–receptor relationships (SRRs) from 1994 to 2021, we analyze the transport history of air masses reaching WNA (25–55° N, 130–90° W). Despite no robust SRR trends within the lower and mid-troposphere (0–8 km), changing emission patterns suggest an intensifying remote influence. Specifically, WNA’s surface NOx emissions have decreased while lower-tail O3 continues to rise, aligning with increasing surface emissions from Southeast Asia and intensified shipping. In contrast, UTLS (8–13 km) SRRs show a clear increase, indicating growing influence from high-altitude sources, including enhanced transport from Southeast Asia and the tropical Pacific, and rising global aircraft emissions. GMI chemical simulations corroborate these findings, revealing that net O3 production over Southeast Asia increased by 157 % in the lower troposphere and 7 % in the free troposphere between 2007 and 2019. The rise in WNA’s low O3 percentiles is driven by the combined influence of intensified transport from Southeast Asia and the tropical Pacific, along with increasing global aircraft and shipping emissions. Ultimately, these trends reflect both the rapid growth of Southeast Asia emissions and shifting trans-Pacific transport.

results.title: Solar Energetic Particle Models: Current Status and Path Forward for Mars L1 Mission Support
results.abstract:
Introduction: The Space Radiation Analysis Group (SRAG) at NASA/Johnson Space Center (JSC) is tasked with the mitigation of impacts of space radiation on the astronaut crew. In addition to instrumentation development and vehicle design analysis, SRAG maintains 24/7 real-time mission support at Mission Control Center-Houston. From the Radiation Console, the team monitors the space environment and measurements from vehicle and crew dosimeters to under-stand the environment and provide recommendations as needed to limit exposure to a level As Low As Reasonably Achievable (ALARA). 

Background: Naturally occurring sources of radiation in space include the van Allen Belts (Trapped Radiation), Galactic Cosmic Radiation (GCR) and Solar Particle Events (SPEs). While SRAG considers the contribution of all 3 sources, real-time console support focuses primarily on SPEs. These transient events are difficult to predict but are relatively easy to shield. Since 2018, SRAG has collaborated with the Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC) and Moon 2 Mars Space Weather Analysis Office (M2M SWAO) to improve our ability to predict prob-ability and intensity of SPEs.

Mission Support: SPE Model Scoreboards developed to date have been integrated into International Space Station (ISS) and Artemis I/II mission operations. Models selected represented a wide variety of techniques, and the Scoreboards provide an ensemble projection to help the console operator characterize and predict the space radiation environment. The team works with the model developers to understand strengths and weaknesses when interpreting the results, and an ongoing end-to-end validation effort confirms the model performance. 

Space Weather Model Implementation for Mars L1: Following the success of ISS and Artemis I/II sup-port, the team is working on a similar Scoreboard for a Mars observer, including space weather model outputs and measurements from Mars-based assets. SRAG has also begun work on the Human-Independent Particle Projection Outlook System (HIPPOS), an Earth-Independent Operations (EIO) tool to accommodate periods of poor communication between the Earth and the vehicle. HIPPOS builds on the current space weather model suite, selecting models applicable to the Mars location and incorporating environmental measurements that can remove the ground from the required communication pathway. The tool will pro-vide a clear output, empowering the crew to act in response to an increase in radiation exposure. An early version of HIPPOS has been accepted for testing in the Moon and Mars Exploration Analogue (MMEA). With these applications of advances in SPE modeling, SRAG is well-positioned to support beyond Low Earth Orbit missions.

This document provides spacecraft owners and operators a reference document describing existing NASA conjunction assessment and collision avoidance practices. Best practices for each topic are described and justified throughout this document by mission phase. results.title: A Ku-band Photonic Based Cloud and Precipitation Radar
results.abstract: Emerging RF photonic technology enables tunable, ultra-wideband, and low phase-noise radio frequency (RF) signal generation and down-conversion while potentially reducing instrument size, weight, and power (SWaP). By utilizing the beat frequency of phase-locked lasers, this innovative approach provides a new pathway for the implementation of remote sensing radar and radiometer systems. This paper describes a prototype Ku-band (13.9 GHz) cloud and precipitation radar based on a RF photonic circuit assembly for technology demonstration. The system architecture, hardware implementation, performance characterization, and measurement results from observations of a thunderstorm system are presented.
